stages.title: What is mathematics?
stages.summary: Before numbers and symbols: what mathematics is, why people invented it, and the kinds of thinking it uses.
stages.why: Everything else rests on these ideas. Counting, comparing, patterns, rules and reasoning are the raw materials of every theorem, including the ones about primes and computation.

stages.title: Understanding numbers
stages.summary: What a number is, how we write numbers, and the families of numbers: whole numbers, negatives, fractions, decimals, primes and more.
stages.why: The Riemann Hypothesis is a statement about prime numbers, and P versus NP is about counting steps. Both start with a clear idea of what a number is.

stages.title: Basic operations
stages.summary: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing - why each operation exists and how it works - then powers, roots and remainders.
stages.why: Operations are the verbs of mathematics. Counting the operations an algorithm performs is the heart of complexity theory; powers and remainders lead to number theory.

stages.title: Learning the language of mathematics
stages.summary: How to read mathematical symbols and say any expression aloud in plain English.
stages.why: Research papers are written in this language. Being able to read notation fluently is what makes advanced mathematics approachable.

stages.title: Introduction to algebra
stages.summary: Letters that stand for numbers, equations that keep both sides balanced, and how to find unknowns.
stages.why: Algebra lets us talk about all numbers at once. Every general statement - every theorem - is written using variables.

stages.title: Graphs, geometry and spatial thinking
stages.summary: Points, lines, shapes, coordinates and graphs: turning numbers into pictures and pictures into numbers.
stages.why: Complex numbers live on a plane, and the zeros of the zeta function are points on it. Graphs of growth make complexity visible.

stages.title: Advanced algebra and functions
stages.summary: Functions as machines that turn inputs into outputs, and the important families of functions.
stages.why: The zeta function is a function; an algorithm's running time is a function. Understanding functions is essential for both destinations.

stages.title: Logic and proof
stages.summary: Statements, truth, implication, quantifiers and the main methods of proof.
stages.why: Research means proving things. Both Millennium problems ask for proofs, and the P versus NP problem is itself partly about the nature of proof.

stages.title: Discrete mathematics
stages.summary: Sets, counting, graphs and Boolean logic - the mathematics of separate, countable things.
stages.why: Computation is discrete. Satisfiability, graph colouring and counting arguments are the everyday tools of complexity theory.

stages.title: Calculus and mathematical analysis
stages.summary: Change, limits, derivatives, integrals and infinite series - first by picture, then rigorously.
stages.why: The zeta function is defined by an infinite series and studied with calculus. Analysis is the language of the Riemann Hypothesis.

stages.title: Number theory
stages.summary: Primes, divisibility, congruences and the functions number theorists use to study them.
stages.why: The Riemann Hypothesis is ultimately a precise statement about how the prime numbers are distributed.

stages.title: Complex numbers
stages.summary: Numbers with a real part and an imaginary part, pictured as points on a plane.
stages.why: The Riemann zeta function takes complex inputs, and the hypothesis says where its zeros lie in the complex plane.

stages.title: Advanced mathematical subjects
stages.summary: The parts of university and graduate mathematics that the two research problems actually need - and nothing extra.
stages.why: Each module below says exactly which destination it serves and why.

modules.title: Real analysis
modules.why: Rigorous limits, convergence and asymptotic notation. Error terms in prime counting and running-time bounds are both stated this way.

modules.title: Linear algebra
modules.why: Matrices and eigenvalues appear in the Hilbert-Polya idea for the Riemann Hypothesis and in algebraic approaches to complexity lower bounds.

modules.title: Abstract algebra
modules.why: Groups, rings and finite fields underlie Dirichlet characters (RH) and algebraic techniques such as algebrization and error-correcting codes (P vs NP).

modules.title: Probability
modules.why: Randomized algorithms and the probabilistic method are central to complexity; random models predict how primes behave.

modules.title: Algorithms and data structures
modules.why: Concrete algorithm design gives intuition for which problems are easy, which seem hard, and why.

modules.title: Computational mathematics
modules.why: Experiments only count as evidence if the computer arithmetic behind them is trustworthy.

modules.title: Numerical analysis
modules.why: Computing zeta zeros accurately - and knowing how accurate the answer is - needs numerical analysis.

modules.title: Mathematical optimization
modules.why: Linear programming is solvable efficiently, integer programming is NP-hard: the boundary is instructive.

modules.title: Complex analysis
modules.why: Holomorphic functions, contour integrals and the argument principle are how mathematicians study and count zeta zeros.

modules.title: Analytic number theory
modules.why: The bridge from the zeta function back to prime numbers.

modules.title: Computational complexity theory (foundations)
modules.why: Turing machines, decidability and diagonalization - the formal setting in which P versus NP is stated.

modules.title: Formal logic
modules.why: First-order logic and formal proof, including machine-checked proofs in Lean 4.

modules.title: Proof theory
modules.why: Proof complexity asks how long proofs must be; it is one of the known routes toward separating complexity classes.

modules.title: Advanced combinatorics and graph theory
modules.why: Extremal set systems and expander graphs drive circuit lower bounds and appear, through graph zeta functions, alongside the Riemann Hypothesis.

stages.title: Research path A: P versus NP
stages.summary: From 'what is an algorithm?' to the frontier of computational complexity theory.
stages.why: P versus NP asks whether every problem whose solutions can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

stages.title: Research path B: The Riemann Hypothesis
stages.summary: From prime numbers to the zeros of the zeta function and the frontier of analytic number theory.
stages.why: The Riemann Hypothesis predicts where the zeros of the zeta function lie, which controls how regularly the primes are spread out. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems.

lessons.title: What is mathematics?
lessons.summary: Mathematics is a language for quantities, patterns, shapes, relationships and logical truths - not just calculation.

lessons.title: Why did humans invent mathematics?
lessons.summary: Keeping track of animals, sharing food, trading and measuring land led people to invent counting and calculation.

lessons.title: What is counting?
lessons.summary: Counting matches each object with one word from a fixed list; the last word says how many.

lessons.title: What is quantity?
lessons.summary: A quantity is 'how much' or 'how many' - something that stays the same when you rearrange things.

lessons.title: What is measurement?
lessons.summary: Measuring is counting how many copies of a chosen unit fit into something.

lessons.title: What is comparison?
lessons.summary: Comparing decides which of two quantities is more, less, or whether they are the same.

lessons.title: What is a mathematical pattern?
lessons.summary: A pattern is a regularity that lets you predict what comes next.

lessons.title: What is a mathematical rule?
lessons.summary: A rule is a precise instruction that always produces the same result from the same starting point.

lessons.title: What is mathematical reasoning?
lessons.summary: Reasoning is reaching conclusions that must be true because of what we already know.

lessons.title: What is a mathematical proof?
lessons.summary: A proof is an argument that shows something is true in every possible case, not just the ones we tried.

lessons.title: Why do mathematical symbols exist?
lessons.summary: Symbols are short, precise names for ideas, which make long sentences quick to write and easy to work with.

lessons.title: How mathematics describes the real world
lessons.summary: A mathematical model describes a real situation with numbers and rules so we can make predictions.

lessons.title: What is a number?
lessons.summary: A number is the idea of 'how many' that all groups of the same size share.

lessons.title: What does counting mean?
lessons.summary: The precise rules of counting: one word per object, always the same order, and the last word answers 'how many?'.

lessons.title: The number zero
lessons.summary: Zero is the number of things in an empty collection, and a placeholder that makes our way of writing numbers work.

lessons.title: One, two, three and beyond
lessons.summary: Every counting number has a next number, so the counting numbers never end.

lessons.title: Counting objects
lessons.summary: Practical counting of larger collections by grouping into tens.

lessons.title: Counting in equal groups
lessons.summary: Counting by twos, threes and fives, and arranging objects in equal rows.

lessons.title: Comparing numbers
lessons.summary: Deciding which of two numbers is larger by pairing objects one-to-one or by counting.

lessons.title: Bigger and smaller
lessons.summary: The symbols > and < and the order of the numbers.

lessons.title: Equal quantities
lessons.summary: What 'equal' really means and the equals sign =.

lessons.title: Number symbols
lessons.summary: The ten digits and place value: why 305 and 35 are different numbers.

lessons.title: Number lines
lessons.summary: Numbers placed in order along a line at equal spacing.

lessons.title: Positive numbers
lessons.summary: Numbers greater than zero, to the right of zero on the number line.

lessons.title: Negative numbers
lessons.summary: Numbers less than zero: temperatures below freezing, depths below sea level, debts.

lessons.title: Whole numbers
lessons.summary: The numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, ... with no parts and no minus sign.

lessons.title: Natural numbers
lessons.summary: The counting numbers, written with the symbol N, and the two conventions about whether 0 is included.

lessons.title: Integers
lessons.summary: All whole numbers and their negatives, written with the symbol Z.

lessons.title: Fractions
lessons.summary: Numbers that describe equal parts of a whole.

lessons.title: Numerators and denominators
lessons.summary: The top number counts parts taken; the bottom number says how many equal parts make a whole.

lessons.title: Decimals
lessons.summary: Place value extended to the right of the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

lessons.title: Percentages
lessons.summary: Percent means 'out of one hundred'.

lessons.title: Ratios
lessons.summary: A ratio compares two quantities, like 2 cups of flour for every 3 eggs.

lessons.title: Composite numbers

lessons.summary: Even numbers split into pairs exactly; odd numbers always leave one over.

lessons.summary: The numbers of equal rows a collection can be arranged into.

lessons.title: Multiples

lessons.title: Divisibility
lessons.summary: When one number shares equally into another with nothing left over.

lessons.title: Greatest common divisors
lessons.summary: The largest number that divides two numbers exactly.

lessons.title: Least common multiples

lessons.title: Addition
lessons.summary: Putting quantities together, and counting on along the number line.

lessons.title: Subtraction

lessons.title: Multiplication

lessons.title: Division

lessons.summary: Strategies for calculating in your head.

lessons.title: What do brackets mean?

lessons.title: What does a square root symbol mean?
lessons.summary: Reading the radical sign and what it asks for.

lessons.title: What does an exponent mean?

lessons.title: What is an unknown number?
lessons.summary: A specific number we have not found yet, given a temporary name.

lessons.summary: A quantity that stays fixed while the variables change.

lessons.summary: A combination of numbers, letters and operations - a mathematical phrase.

lessons.title: What is an equation?
lessons.summary: A mathematical sentence saying two expressions are equal.

lessons.title: What is an inequality?
lessons.summary: A sentence saying one expression is bigger or smaller than another.

lessons.title: How to substitute numbers
lessons.summary: Replacing letters by numbers to find an expression's value.

l0-comparison.goal: We are learning what it means to compare two quantities, and three reliable ways to do it.
l0-comparison.why:
"Is there more?", "Is this bigger?", "Is it the same?" are among the first questions anyone
asks. Every inequality, every ranking, and every statement that one algorithm is faster than
another is a comparison.
l0-comparison.problem: How do you decide, with certainty, which of two amounts is bigger - or whether they are equal?
l0-comparison.plain:
Comparing two quantities means finding out which of three things is true:

- the first is **more** than the second,
- they are **the same**,
- the first is **less** than the second.

Exactly one of these is always true - never two at once, and never none.

There are three reliable ways to compare:

1. **Side by side** - stand two children back to back to see who is taller.
2. **Matching** - pair the objects of two groups one-to-one. Whichever group has objects left
   over is bigger. If nothing is left over, they are the same.
3. **Counting or measuring** - find a number for each, then compare the numbers.

One warning: you can only compare quantities **of the same kind**. Three watermelons and five
grapes - "more" what? More fruit (five is more), or more weight (the watermelons win)?

analogy.title: Back to back
analogy.text:
Two friends stand back to back on flat ground and a third friend lays a book flat across the
tops of their heads. If the book tilts, one is taller. If it sits level, they are the same
height. Nobody needed a ruler - just a direct comparison.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: two groups of objects, one on the left and one on the right. Lines pair
each object on the left with one on the right. Objects with no partner are highlighted. The
group with unpartnered objects is the bigger group.
visual.prompt: Add or remove objects on either side and watch the matching change.

example_simple.title: Apples and pears
example_simple.problem: There are 5 apples and 3 pears. Which group is bigger?
steps: Pair each pear with an apple - 3 pairs.
2 apples are left without a partner.
example_simple.answer: There are more apples than pears.

example_harder.title: More of what?
example_harder.problem: A child has 3 big watermelons. Another has 5 grapes. Who has more fruit?
steps: The question is unclear, because "more" could mean two different quantities.
*More pieces of fruit?* Count them: 5 grapes is more than 3 watermelons.
*More weight of fruit?* Weigh them: 3 watermelons are much heavier than 5 grapes.
To compare, we must first agree which quantity we are comparing.
example_harder.answer: It depends on the quantity. By number, the grapes win; by weight, the watermelons win.

word.text:
This is called **comparison**. When we compare, we use the words **more** (or *greater*,
*bigger*), **fewer** or **less** (*smaller*), and **the same** (*equal*). Strictly, "fewer" is
used for things you count ("fewer apples") and "less" for things you measure ("less water"),
though many people use "less" for both.

l0-comparison.no_symbol_note:
Mathematics has special symbols for "greater than", "less than" and "equal to": $>$, $<$ and $=$.
You will meet them properly in [[lesson:l1-bigger-smaller|Bigger and smaller]] and
[[lesson:l1-equal-quantities|Equal quantities]].

formal.statement:
To **compare** two quantities of the same kind is to determine which one of three possibilities
holds: the first is greater than the second, the two are equal, or the first is less than the
second.

glossary.meaning: Both are numbers of things, or both are lengths, or both are weights - not a mixture.
More than.
Exactly the same amount.
Smaller than, or fewer than.

connections_back.how: We compare quantities - how many or how much.
Matching one-to-one is the oldest way to compare groups.

worked.title: Plates and guests
worked.problem: You are laying a table. You put one plate in front of each chair, and two plates are left in your hands. What can you say about plates and chairs?
steps: Putting one plate per chair is a one-to-one matching.
Every chair got a plate, and 2 plates had no chair.
worked.answer: There are more plates than chairs - exactly 2 more.

experiment.task: Change the groups until they are exactly the same size, so every object has a partner.
experiment.success:
When every object has exactly one partner, the groups are equal. Notice you did not have to
count - matching alone decided it.

mistakes.mistake: Judging "more" by how much space a group takes up.
mistakes.why: Spread-out objects look like more. Spacing is not quantity.
mistakes.fix: Match one-to-one, or count.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing quantities of different kinds.
mistakes.why: "More" is meaningless unless you say more of what - number, length, weight, time.
mistakes.fix: First decide which quantity you are comparing.

statements.text: For any two counting numbers, exactly one of these is true - the first is smaller, they are equal, or the first is bigger.
statements.note: This is called the law of trichotomy. It can be proved from the basic rules of arithmetic.

questions.prompt: You pair up cats and dogs, one cat with each dog. Three dogs have no cat. What do you know?
questions.explanation: The group with objects left over is bigger, so there are more dogs - three more.

options.text: There are more dogs than cats.
There are more cats than dogs.
options.diagnosis: The animals left without a partner belong to the bigger group - those are the dogs.

options.text: There are the same number of each.
options.diagnosis: Equal groups pair up with nothing left over. Here three dogs are left.

questions.prompt: When you compare two counting numbers, how many of the three possibilities (more, equal, less) are true?
questions.explanation: Exactly one of more, equal or less is always true.

options.diagnosis: Two amounts cannot be equal and different at once, or each bigger than the other.
Two counting numbers always stand in one of the three relations.

questions.prompt: True or false: "3 metres is more than 5 kilograms" is a sensible comparison.
questions.explanation: False. We can only compare quantities of the same kind.
questions.diagnosis: Length and weight are different kinds of quantity - one cannot be "more" than the other.

questions.prompt: You give one sticker to each child in a group. You have 9 stickers and 2 are left over. How many children are in the group?
questions.hint: Each child got one sticker, and 2 stickers had nobody.
questions.explanation: 9 stickers, 2 unused, so 7 stickers were matched with 7 children.

common_wrong.diagnosis: The 2 leftover stickers had no child, so there are fewer children than stickers.

questions.prompt: Describe a way to find out which of two groups of objects is bigger without counting either group.
questions.explanation: One-to-one matching compares groups without counting.
rubric: Pair the objects one-to-one.
The group with objects left over is bigger.
If nothing is left over, the groups are equal.
questions.model_answer:
Pair them up: match one object from the first group with one from the second, again and
again. If one group has objects left over at the end, it is the bigger group. If everything
pairs off with nothing left, the groups are the same size.

connections_forward.how: Comparing numbers by matching and by counting.
The symbols for greater than and less than.
Chains of comparisons let us reason about things we never compared directly.
Complexity theory compares how quickly the running times of algorithms grow.

alternatives.title: The fair party
alternatives.text:
Two teams each claim to have brought more balloons to a party. Instead of arguing, the host
asks one member of each team to step forward together, each holding one balloon, and pop
them into a shared box - one from each side, over and over. When the blue team runs out, the
red team still has two balloons. Everyone can now see that red brought more - and by
exactly two. Nobody counted; the matching settled the argument.

alternatives.title: Three questions in a row
alternatives.text:
When comparing two groups, ask in this order:

1. **Are they the same kind of thing?** (Both counts? Both lengths?) If not, stop - they cannot be compared.
2. **Can I put them side by side or pair them up?** If yes, do it and look for leftovers.
3. **If not, can I count or measure both?** Then compare the two numbers.

Each question is small, and together they always give an answer.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
You have some red blocks and some blue blocks. Put one red block on top of each blue block.
Are there any red blocks left over? Then there are more red ones! Any blue ones left
without a red block on top? Then there are more blue ones! Nothing left over? Then they are
the same!

l0-counting.goal:
We are learning what counting really is: matching each object with one word from a fixed
list, so that the last word tells you how many.
l0-counting.why:
Pebbles work, but they are slow and heavy. Counting does the same job with words you carry in
your head. Almost every later idea - numbers, adding, even counting the steps of a computer
program - starts here.
l0-counting.problem: How do you find out *how many* things there are, quickly and reliably, and tell someone else?
l0-counting.plain:
When you count, you do three things at once:

1. You point at each object **exactly once**.
2. You say the counting words **in the same order every time**: one, two, three, four, ...
3. The **last word you say** tells you how many objects there are.

Counting is the shepherd's pebbles, but with words instead of pebbles. Each object gets
matched with one word. Because everybody learns the counting words in the same order, the last
word is a name for "how many" that everyone understands.

One surprising fact: it does not matter where you start or which order you go in. Count
the same objects any way you like and - if you are careful - you always get the same answer.

analogy.title: Raffle tickets
analogy.text:
Imagine giving out raffle tickets numbered 1, 2, 3, ... to people as they arrive, one
ticket each. When the last person arrives, the number on their ticket tells you how many
people came. Counting is exactly this - each object receives the next "ticket" (counting
word), and the last ticket number is the total.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a tray of apples. When you tap an apple it receives the next counting
number - the first apple you tap gets 1, the next gets 2, and so on. Each apple can only be
tapped once. The last number given out is how many apples are on the tray.
visual.prompt: Tap every apple. Then press "Start again" and count them in a different order.

example_simple.title: Four cups
example_simple.problem: How many cups are on the shelf? (There are four.)
steps: Point at the first cup and say "one".
Point at the next cup and say "two".
Point at the next cup and say "three".
Point at the last cup and say "four". There are no cups left without a word.
example_simple.answer: The last word was "four", so there are four cups.

example_harder.title: A messy pile of shells
example_harder.problem: Shells are scattered on a table, not in a line. How can you count them without missing any or counting one twice?
steps: The danger with a messy pile is losing track of which shells already have a word.
Fix it by moving each shell to the side as you say its word - counted shells go left, uncounted stay right.
Keep going until no uncounted shells remain.
The last word you said is the number of shells.
example_harder.answer: Separate counted from uncounted objects as you go. That guarantees each object gets exactly one word.

word.text:
The name for this activity is **counting**, and the ordered list of words - one, two,
three, ... - is called the **counting sequence**. Different languages use different words
(*un, deux, trois* in French; *ichi, ni, san* in Japanese), but the method is the same
everywhere.

l0-counting.no_symbol_note:
Counting uses words. The written symbols for those words - 1, 2, 3 and so on - are the
subject of [[lesson:l1-number-symbols|Number symbols]] in Level 1.

formal.statement:
To **count** a collection is to match its objects one-to-one with the counting words
"one, two, three, ...", taken in their fixed order and starting from "one". The last word
used is called the **number** of objects in the collection.

glossary.meaning: The group of objects being counted.
Each object gets exactly one word, and each word is used for exactly one object.
The counting words are always said in the same sequence.
The answer to "how many?" - here, the last counting word used.

connections_back.how: Counting is one-to-one correspondence between objects and the counting words, instead of objects and pebbles.

worked.title: Stars in a circle
worked.problem: Seven stars are drawn in a circle. When you count around the circle, how do you know when to stop?
steps: In a circle there is no natural first or last star, so it is easy to go round twice.
Before you start, mark the starting star (put your finger next to it).
Count around, one star per word.
Stop when you reach the star *before* your marked star - the next one has already been counted.
worked.answer: Mark where you began. You will say "seven" on the star just before the marked one.

experiment.task: Count all the stars by tapping each one. Then press "Shuffle" and count again in a different order.
experiment.success:
However you count, the last number is always the same. That is why counting gives an answer
everyone can agree on: the total does not depend on the order you count in.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping an object or counting one twice.
mistakes.why: Then the matching is not one-to-one, so the last word is not the true total.
mistakes.fix: Move or mark each object as you count it.

mistakes.mistake: Saying the words faster than you point.
mistakes.why: Your words and objects drift out of step, so some objects get two words and some get none.
mistakes.fix: Touch each object as you say its word - one touch, one word.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking the last word names only the last object ("that one is the fifth, not five things").
mistakes.why: The last word does two jobs - it labels the last object *and* tells you the total.
mistakes.fix: After counting, wave at the whole group and say "five apples" - the word describes all of them.

statements.text: Psychologists Rochel Gelman and Randy Gallistel (1978) described the principles children must grasp to count correctly, including one word per object, a stable order of words, and the last word giving the total.
Counting a finite collection in any order gives the same final number.
statements.note: Mathematicians prove this from the definition of counting; it is why counting is reliable.

questions.prompt: You count 8 shells. Then your friend counts the same shells, starting from a different shell. If you both count carefully, what will your friend get?
questions.explanation: Counting in a different order always gives the same total - 8.

options.diagnosis: The order of counting never changes the total, as long as every shell gets exactly one word.
Starting somewhere else changes which shell is "first", not how many shells there are.

questions.prompt: True or false: when you count 5 toys, the word "five" describes only the last toy you touched.
questions.explanation: False. "Five" is the number of toys in the whole group.
questions.diagnosis: The last counting word tells you how many there are altogether - it describes the whole group.

questions.prompt: Mia counts her marbles one at a time and the last word she says is "twelve". How many marbles does she have?
questions.explanation: The last counting word is the total, so Mia has 12 marbles.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words what you must do so that counting gives the right answer.
questions.explanation: Correct counting needs one word per object, the fixed order of words, and reading the total from the last word.
rubric: Each object gets exactly one counting word (none skipped, none counted twice).
The counting words are said in their usual order.
The last word said is the number of objects.
questions.model_answer:
You have to give each object exactly one counting word - no skipping and no counting
twice - and say the words in the usual order: one, two, three, ... Then the last word
you say is how many objects there are.

connections_forward.how: Counting measures a quantity - how many.
In Level 1 we look at the precise rules of counting and the idea of cardinality.
Complexity theory, the field of P versus NP, begins by counting the steps a computation takes.

alternatives.title: One idea at a time
alternatives.text:
Let's split counting into three tiny jobs.

**Job 1 - say the words in order.** Practise just saying: one, two, three, four, five.
Always the same order.

**Job 2 - one word per thing.** Put three spoons in a row. Touch the first and say a word,
touch the second and say the next word, touch the third and say the next word. Touch and
word happen together.

**Job 3 - the last word is the answer.** After touching the last spoon, the word you just
said ("three") is how many spoons there are.

Counting is just doing all three jobs at once.

alternatives.title: Reciting is not counting
alternatives.text:
A small child can often say "one, two, three, four, five, six" perfectly - but when asked
"how many teddies?" they may point at random and say any word. Saying the words in order is
*reciting*. *Counting* is matching each teddy with exactly one of those words. The
difference is the matching. Without it, the words are just a song.

alternatives.title: The careless gardener
alternatives.text:
A gardener counted the apple trees in her orchard while walking in circles, and got 23 one
day and 26 the next. A friend suggested tying a ribbon to each tree as she counted it. Now
she got 24 every time. The ribbons made sure each tree received exactly one counting word -
and that is the whole secret of counting.

l0-measurement.goal: We are learning that measuring means choosing a unit and counting how many of that unit fit.
l0-measurement.why:
Some quantities - length, weight, time - cannot be counted one by one, because they do not
come in separate pieces. Measurement turns them into counting by choosing a "piece" to count
with. That one idea lets mathematics describe the physical world.
l0-measurement.problem:
How do you answer "how long is this table?" in a way that someone on the other side of the
world will understand exactly?
l0-measurement.plain:
To measure something:

1. **Choose a unit** - a fixed amount to use as "one": a paperclip, a footstep, a centimetre.
2. **Count how many units fit** along (or into) the thing you are measuring.

A pencil that is "6 paperclips long" has had paperclips laid end to end along it, and 6 fitted.

The number you get **depends on the unit**. With a longer unit fewer fit; with a shorter unit
more fit. So a measurement is always two things together: a number *and* a unit. "6" on its own
means nothing; "6 paperclips" or "6 centimetres" means something exact.

This is why the world agreed on standard units such as the metre and the kilogram: if everyone
uses the same unit, everyone gets the same number.

analogy.title: Footsteps across a room
analogy.text:
Walk across a room heel-to-toe and count your footsteps: perhaps 14. A small child does the
same and counts 20. You are both right - your feet are different units. If you both used the
same ruler instead of your own feet, you would agree.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a pencil, with a row of identical units laid end to end beside it. The
number shows how many units fit along the pencil. Choose a different unit and the number
changes - but the pencil stays exactly the same length.
visual.prompt: Measure the pencil in paperclips, then in finger-widths, then in centimetres.

example_simple.title: A book measured in paperclips
example_simple.problem: Paperclips are laid end to end along a book, and 8 of them fit exactly. How long is the book?
steps: The unit is one paperclip.
Eight units fit along the book.

example_harder.title: Two measurements, both right
example_harder.problem: Sam measures a table and gets 10 hand-spans. His mother measures the same table and gets 8 hand-spans. Who is right?
steps: They used different units - Sam's hand-span is shorter than his mother's.
A shorter unit fits more times, so Sam gets a bigger number.
Both measurements are correct for the unit used. The problem is that "hand-span" is not a fixed unit.
If they both used centimetres, they would get the same number.
example_harder.answer: Both are right. Different units give different numbers - which is why standard units exist.

word.text:
This process is called **measurement**, and the fixed amount you count with is called a
**unit**. Standard units have names and short symbols: the **metre** (m) and **centimetre**
(cm) for length, the **kilogram** (kg) for weight, the **second** (s) for time.

symbols.name: centimetre
symbols.looks_like: The two letters c and m, written after a number.
symbols.means: A unit of length equal to one hundredth of a metre - about the width of a fingernail.
symbols.why: Writing "cm" is much shorter than "centimetres", and the same abbreviation is used in almost every country.

formal.statement:
To **measure** a quantity is to compare it with a fixed reference quantity of the same kind,
called a **unit**, and to express it as the number of units (and parts of a unit) it equals.
A measurement therefore consists of a number together with a unit.

glossary.meaning: To see how one amount relates to another - here, how many units fit.
An agreed amount used as a standard, such as one metre.
Lengths are measured with a unit of length, weights with a unit of weight.
When the unit does not fit a whole number of times - this leads to fractions.

notation.read_aloud: fifteen centimetres
notation.english: Fifteen copies of a centimetre, laid end to end, are as long as the thing measured.

connections_back.how: Length, weight and time are "how much" quantities, found by measuring.
Measuring is counting units.

worked.title: A bigger unit
worked.problem: A rope is 12 paperclips long. A "double clip" is two paperclips joined end to end. How long is the rope in double clips?
steps: Each double clip covers the same length as 2 paperclips.
Group the 12 paperclips in twos along the rope - each pair is one double clip.
Counting the pairs gives 6.
worked.answer: 6 double clips. A unit twice as long fits half as many times.

experiment.task: Measure the rope with every unit available. Which unit gives the biggest number, and why?
experiment.success:
The smallest unit gave the biggest number, because more small units fit along the same rope.
The rope never changed. A measurement only makes sense together with its unit.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving out the unit ("the table is 150").
mistakes.why: 150 what? Centimetres, paperclips and footsteps give very different tables.
mistakes.fix: Always say the number *and* the unit - "150 centimetres".

mistakes.mistake: Leaving gaps or overlaps between units when measuring.
mistakes.why: Gaps make the count too small; overlaps make it too big.
mistakes.fix: Lay units end to end, touching but not overlapping, starting exactly at one end.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking two different measurements of the same thing mean one person is wrong.
mistakes.why: They may have used different units.
mistakes.fix: Check the units first. Convert to the same unit before comparing.

statements.text: Since 1983, the metre has been defined as the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
statements.note: Defining a unit this way means anyone, anywhere, can reproduce exactly the same metre.

statements.text: Which unit we choose is a convention. The thing being measured does not change when we change units.

questions.prompt: A complete measurement must include...
questions.explanation: A measurement is a number together with a unit, such as 8 cm.

options.diagnosis: A number alone does not say what was counted. "8" could be 8 centimetres or 8 metres.
A unit alone does not say how many fit.

questions.prompt: True or false: if two people measure the same table and get different numbers, one of them must have made a mistake.
questions.explanation: False. Different units give different numbers for the same length.
questions.diagnosis: They may simply have used different units, such as their own hand-spans.

questions.prompt: A path is 10 footsteps long. A giant's footstep is exactly as long as 2 of your footsteps. How many giant footsteps long is the path?
questions.explanation: Each giant step covers 2 of your steps, so 10 steps make 5 giant steps.

common_wrong.diagnosis: A bigger unit fits *fewer* times, not more. Each giant step covers two of yours.
Adding 2 does not work. Group your footsteps in twos - each pair is one giant step.

questions.prompt: You measure a door with a long unit, then with a shorter unit. What happens to the number you get?
questions.explanation: Shorter units fit more times, so the number gets bigger.

options.text: It gets bigger, because more short units fit.

options.diagnosis: Shorter units each cover less, so you need more of them.
The door stays the same length, but the number of units that fit changes.

questions.prompt: Explain to someone why "the room is 20 long" is not a good answer, and how to fix it.
questions.explanation: Measurements need units, because the number depends on the unit chosen.
rubric: It is missing a unit.
Different units give different numbers, so 20 alone is unclear.
Fix it by saying the unit, such as 20 footsteps or 5 metres.
questions.model_answer:
"20" does not say what was counted - 20 footsteps, 20 metres and 20 paperclips are very
different lengths. A measurement needs a unit, so you should say something like "the room
is 20 footsteps long" or, better, use a standard unit like metres.

connections_forward.how: Measuring lets us compare quantities that cannot be put side by side.
When a unit does not fit an exact number of times, we need parts of units - fractions.
Area is measured by counting unit squares.

alternatives.title: Measure your desk three ways
alternatives.text:
Measure the width of a table using (1) your hand-span, (2) a spoon, and (3) a book, laying
each one end to end. Write down the three numbers *with their units*: "9 hand-spans", "14
spoons", "4 books". The table did not change, but the numbers did. Each measurement answered
the question "how many of these fit?" - and that is all measurement ever is.

alternatives.title: Why the metre was invented
alternatives.text:
For centuries, lengths were measured with body parts - feet, hands, thumbs - and every town
had its own version, which made trading confusing and unfair. In the 1790s, French scientists
defined a new unit, the metre, as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the
equator, so that it belonged to no single country. Today the metre is defined using the speed
of light, so it can be reproduced exactly anywhere. The aim was always the same: one unit that
everyone shares.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
How long is your teddy bear? Let's line up toy blocks next to it: one, two, three, four, five
blocks! Your teddy is "5 blocks long". If we used tiny buttons instead, we might count 15
buttons - more, because buttons are smaller. Measuring is just counting how many of
something fit.

l0-patterns.goal:
We are learning what a mathematical pattern is, how to continue one - and why patterns can
fool you.
l0-patterns.why:
Noticing patterns is how most mathematics is discovered. People noticed that the primes thin
out in a particular way long before anyone could explain it - and that pattern eventually led
to the Riemann Hypothesis. But patterns also mislead, which is why mathematics needs proof.
l0-patterns.problem:
When you see a few things in a row, how can you predict what comes next - and how sure can
you be?
l0-patterns.plain:
A **pattern** is something that repeats or grows in a regular way, so that you can predict
what comes next.

- A **repeating pattern** goes round and round: red, blue, red, blue, red, ...
- A **growing pattern** changes by a regular rule: 2, 4, 6, 8, ... (two more each time).

To continue a pattern, look for *what stays the same* about how one item becomes the next.

But be careful: a pattern you have seen a few times might not continue forever. Seeing a
pattern is a **guess** - a very useful guess, but still a guess - until someone explains *why*
it must continue.

analogy.title: Music and wallpaper
analogy.text:
A drum beat - boom, tap, tap, boom, tap, tap - is a repeating pattern: once you have heard it,
you can clap along. Wallpaper with flowers every hand-width is the same idea in space. Your
brain predicts what comes next without being told. Mathematics makes that prediction precise.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a growing pattern of dots arranged in squares - 1 dot, then 4, then 9,
then 16. Each picture is the next "stage" of the pattern. Before revealing the next stage, try
to predict how many dots it will have.
visual.prompt: Predict the next stage, then reveal it. Try the other patterns too.

example_simple.title: Counting by twos
example_simple.problem: What comes next - 2, 4, 6, 8, ...?
steps: Look at how each number becomes the next. 2 to 4 is two more. 4 to 6 is two more. 6 to 8 is two more.
The pattern is "two more each time".
Two more than 8 is 10.

example_harder.title: The growing triangle
example_harder.problem: Dots are arranged in triangles - 1, 3, 6, 10. How many dots are in the next triangle?
steps: The differences are not all the same - 1 to 3 is two more, 3 to 6 is three more, 6 to 10 is four more.
But the differences themselves form a pattern - 2, 3, 4, ... - each one more than the last.
So the next difference should be 5, and 10 + 5 = 15.
In the picture each new triangle adds a new bottom row, one dot longer than the last row - which explains *why* the pattern continues.
example_harder.answer: 15 dots. The pattern was hidden one layer deeper, in the differences.

word.text:
The word is **pattern**. Each item in a pattern is often called a **term** or a **stage**:
in 2, 4, 6, 8 the first term is 2 and the fourth term is 8.

symbols.name: ellipsis
symbols.looks_like: Three dots in a row, sitting on the line like full stops.
symbols.means: "And so on, following the same pattern" - the list continues in the way it has started.
symbols.why: Writing a pattern out forever is impossible. The ellipsis says "you can see how it continues" in three dots.

formal.statement:
A **pattern** is a regularity in an ordered list of objects or numbers that can be described
by a rule, so that later items can be predicted from earlier ones. A pattern observed in
finitely many cases is a guess about later cases, not a guarantee.

glossary.meaning: Something that happens in the same way again and again.
Items in a definite order - first, second, third, ...
An exact description of how to get the items.
Only the cases actually looked at - not all possible ones.

notation.read_aloud: two, four, six, eight, and so on

parts.meaning: The first four terms of the pattern.
The list continues in the same way forever.

notation.english: The numbers that go up by two each time, starting from two, without end.

connections_back.how: Counting itself is a pattern - each counting word is one more than the last.

worked.title: The pattern that breaks
worked.problem: Put 1, 2, 3, 4 and then 5 points on a circle and join every pair of points with straight lines. The circle is cut into 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 pieces. How many pieces will 6 points give?
steps: The numbers 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 seem to double each time, so it is very tempting to predict 32.
But when you actually draw 6 points carefully, the most pieces you can get is 31.
The doubling pattern held for five cases and then broke.
The pattern was a coincidence of small cases, not a rule.
worked.answer: 31, not 32. A pattern seen in a few cases can fail - which is exactly why mathematics needs proof.

experiment.task: Choose a pattern, predict the next stage before revealing it, and get three predictions right.
experiment.success:
You found the rule behind each pattern and used it to predict. Each time you made a
prediction, you were making a guess based on a rule you believed - mathematics then asks,
"can we be *sure* the rule continues?"

mistakes.mistake: Assuming that because a pattern held a few times, it must hold forever.
mistakes.why: Some patterns break - like the circle pieces that go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31.
mistakes.fix: Treat a pattern as a guess until you understand *why* it continues.

mistakes.mistake: Looking only at the numbers and not at how they change.
mistakes.why: The pattern is often in the differences, as in 1, 3, 6, 10.
mistakes.fix: Write down how each term turns into the next.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking a short list has only one possible continuation.
mistakes.why: 1, 2, 4 could continue 8 (doubling) or 7 (adding 1, then 2, then 3, ...).
mistakes.fix: Ask what rule produced the list. Without the rule, several continuations are possible.

statements.text: Joining all pairs of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 points on a circle gives at most 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 pieces.
"Joining points on a circle always doubles the number of pieces."
statements.note: With 6 points the maximum is 31, not 32. Five cases of a pattern did not make it true.

questions.prompt: What comes next: 3, 6, 9, 12, ...?
questions.explanation: Each term is 3 more than the one before, so 12 + 3 = 15.

common_wrong.diagnosis: The pattern goes up by 3 each time, not 1.

questions.prompt: Triangles of dots have 1, 3, 6, 10, 15 dots. How many dots does the next triangle have?
questions.hint: Look at how much is added each time.
questions.explanation: The amount added grows by one each time (2, 3, 4, 5, then 6), so 15 + 6 = 21.

common_wrong.diagnosis: The differences grow by one each time - 2, 3, 4, 5 - so the next difference is 6.
Look at the differences between terms - 2, 3, 4, 5. The next one is 6.

questions.prompt: A pattern goes: circle, square, square, circle, square, square, circle, ... What is the next shape?
questions.explanation: The block "circle, square, square" repeats, so after a circle comes a square.

options.diagnosis: After each circle come two squares. The last shape shown was a circle, so a square comes next.

questions.prompt: True or false: if a pattern works for the first five cases, it must work forever.
questions.explanation: False. Patterns can break. Only a proof shows a pattern continues forever.
questions.diagnosis: Remember the circle pieces - 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and then 31. Five cases did not guarantee the sixth.

questions.prompt: Describe in your own words the rule for 5, 10, 15, 20, ... and say what the 6th term is.
questions.explanation: The rule is "start at 5 and add 5 each time"; the 6th term is 30.
rubric: Each term is 5 more than the one before (or counting in fives).
The pattern starts at 5.
The 6th term is 30.
questions.model_answer: Start at 5 and add 5 each time - counting in fives. The terms are 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, so the 6th term is 30.

connections_forward.how: A rule is the exact description that produces a pattern.
Proof is how we become sure a pattern continues.
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers - patterns made precise.
The pattern in how prime numbers thin out leads to the Riemann Hypothesis.

alternatives.title: Build it with coins
alternatives.text:
Make a row of 1 coin. Under it, a row of 2 coins. Under that, 3 coins. You have built a
triangle: 1, then 1 + 2 = 3 coins, then 3 + 3 = 6 coins. Before adding the next row, predict
the total - then build it and check. Building the pattern shows you *why* it grows the way it
does: each new row is one coin longer than the last.

alternatives.title: Pattern or coincidence?
alternatives.text:
Compare two lists.

- 2, 4, 6, 8, ... comes from a clear rule ("two more each time"). We can see why it continues.
- The scores of a football team in four matches, 2, 4, 6, 8, came from four games. There is
  no rule making the next score 10.

Both lists *look* the same. The difference is whether a rule produces them. A mathematical
pattern is one backed by a rule.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
Clap, clap, stomp. Clap, clap, stomp. Clap, clap, ... what comes next? Stomp! You knew
because it keeps doing the same thing over and over. That is a pattern. Mathematicians love
patterns because they let you guess what comes next - and then they try to find out *why*,
so they can be really sure.

l0-proof.goal:
We are learning what a mathematical proof is, why examples are not enough, and how a single
counterexample can destroy a claim.
l0-proof.why:
Proof is what makes mathematical knowledge permanent. A theorem proved 2,300 years ago is still
true today and will be true forever. The Riemann Hypothesis and P versus NP are famous precisely
because nobody has managed to *prove* them - although huge amounts of evidence exist.
l0-proof.problem:
How can you be certain a statement is true for *every* case, when there are infinitely many
cases and you can only check a few?
l0-proof.plain:
A **proof** is an explanation that shows a statement is true in **every possible case** - not
just the cases you happened to check.

Checking examples is useful: it helps you believe something and understand it. But examples
can never cover infinitely many cases. Remember the circle pieces: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16... and then
31. Five examples agreed with "doubling", and the sixth did not.

A proof works differently. Instead of checking cases one by one, it explains a **reason** that
applies to all cases at once.

The opposite also matters. To show that a claim about "every" case is **false**, you need just
**one** case where it fails. That one case is called a **counterexample**.

- A statement that has been proved is a **theorem**.
- A statement that people believe but have not proved is a **conjecture**.

analogy.title: Testing a bridge versus understanding it
analogy.text:
Driving ten heavy lorries over a new bridge shows it held those ten lorries. It does not show
it will hold the eleventh. An engineer who calculates exactly how the steel carries the weight
can say "it will hold any lorry up to 40 tonnes" - and explain why. Examples are like the test
drives; a proof is like the engineer's calculation that covers every case.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: two even numbers drawn as dots arranged in pairs (two rows). When the two
groups are pushed together, every dot still has a partner, because pairs joined to pairs are
still pairs. The table records each example you try. The argument underneath explains why
it *must* work for every even number, not just these.
visual.prompt: Try several pairs of even numbers. Then read the argument and ask whether any example could break it.

example_simple.title: Even plus even
example_simple.problem: Is the sum of two even numbers always even?
steps: Checking examples first - 2 + 4 = 6, 8 + 10 = 18, 12 + 6 = 18. All even. Encouraging, but only three cases.
Now the reason. An even number is one that can be arranged entirely in pairs, with nothing left over.
Take any two even numbers. Both groups of dots are made entirely of pairs.
Putting the two groups together gives a group made entirely of pairs - nothing can be left over, because nothing was left over in either group.
So the total is even. The reason did not depend on which even numbers we chose.
example_simple.answer: Yes - and now we know it for every pair of even numbers, not just the ones we tried. That is a proof.

example_harder.title: Every odd number is prime?
example_harder.problem: Someone notices that 3, 5 and 7 are odd, and each is a prime number (it cannot be split into equal rows except one row). They claim - "every odd number bigger than 1 is prime". Is this true?
steps: The claim is about *every* odd number, so one failure is enough to destroy it.
Try the next odd number - 9.
9 dots can be arranged as 3 equal rows of 3.
So 9 is not prime, even though it is odd.
example_harder.answer: The claim is false. 9 is a counterexample - one example is enough to disprove an "every" claim.

word.text:
An argument that settles a statement for every case is a **proof**. One case that breaks an
"every" statement is a **counterexample**. A statement that has been proved is a **theorem**
(from Greek *theōrēma*, "something looked at"). A statement believed but not yet proved is a
**conjecture** (from Latin *conicere*, "to throw together" - an educated guess).

symbols.name: end-of-proof mark
symbols.looks_like: A small filled-in square at the end of a line.
symbols.means: "The proof is finished."
symbols.why: Proofs can be long. The square tells the reader exactly where the argument ends. Older books write "Q.E.D." instead - Latin for "which was to be demonstrated".
symbols.read_aloud: "End of proof", or "Q.E.D." (say the three letters).

formal.statement:
A **proof** of a statement is a finite sequence of steps, each of which is an accepted
assumption, a definition, a previously proved result, or follows logically from earlier steps,
and whose final step is the statement itself.

glossary.meaning: A list of steps that ends - a proof cannot go on forever.
A starting fact everyone agrees to use.
A theorem that has already been proved and can be reused.
Must be true if the earlier steps are true.

notation.read_aloud: even plus even equals even - end of proof

parts.meaning: Any even number at all - not one particular number.

notation.english: Whichever two even numbers you choose, their total is even - and this has been proved.

connections_back.how: A proof is a complete chain of reasoning.
Patterns suggest what to prove; proof tells us whether the pattern really continues.

worked.title: Checking a claim
worked.problem: Claim - "every number made of the same digit repeated, like 22, 333 or 4444, is divisible by its digit" (for example 333 shares exactly into 3 groups of 111). Is it a theorem, a conjecture, or false?
steps: Check examples - 22 is 2 groups of 11. 333 is 3 groups of 111. 4444 is 4 groups of 1111. All work.
Look for the reason. A number like 4444 is four copies of 1111 added together, so it splits into 4 equal groups of 1111.
The same reason works for any repeated digit - "ddd...d" is d copies of "111...1".
So the reason covers every case.
worked.answer: It is true for every case, and the reason we found is a proof - so it is a theorem.

experiment.task: Try at least three different pairs of even numbers. Then try to find two even numbers whose total is odd.
experiment.success:
You could not find a counterexample - and the pairs argument explains why none exists. Every
example agreed with the theorem, but it is the *reason*, not the examples, that makes it certain.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking that many examples prove a statement.
mistakes.why: Examples cover only the cases checked. A statement about infinitely many numbers needs a reason that covers all of them.
mistakes.fix: Use examples to build belief and understanding, then look for the reason.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking one counterexample is "just an exception".
mistakes.why: An "every" statement is false if even one case fails. There are no exceptions in mathematics.
mistakes.fix: If you find a counterexample, the statement must be changed or dropped.

mistakes.mistake: Calling a well-supported conjecture a theorem.
mistakes.why: Evidence, however strong, is not proof.
mistakes.fix: Say "conjecture" until a proof exists - as with the Riemann Hypothesis.

statements.text: The sum of two even numbers is always even.
Every odd number greater than 1 is prime.
statements.note: 9 is a counterexample: 9 = 3 rows of 3.

statements.text: There are infinitely many prime numbers.
statements.note: Proved by Euclid around 300 BCE. You will study the proof in Level 10.

statements.text: Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two prime numbers (Goldbach's conjecture, 1742).
Goldbach's conjecture has been checked by computer for every even number up to 4 × 10¹⁸ (four billion billion).
statements.note: This enormous evidence is still not a proof - which is why Goldbach's statement is still a conjecture.

questions.prompt: You check a statement about numbers in 5 examples, and it works every time. What do you know?
questions.explanation: Examples show the statement holds in those cases only. A proof is needed for all cases.

options.text: It is true in those 5 cases, but it might fail in some other case.
It is true for every number.
options.diagnosis: Five examples cannot cover every number. Remember the circle pieces - 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, then 31.
Nothing has gone wrong yet - but nothing has been proved either.

questions.prompt: True or false: one counterexample is enough to show that a statement about "every" case is false.
questions.explanation: True. One case that fails is enough.
questions.diagnosis: An "every" statement claims no exceptions, so a single exception destroys it.

questions.prompt: Which number is a counterexample to the claim "every odd number is bigger than 2"?
questions.explanation: 1 is odd but not bigger than 2, so it breaks the claim.

options.diagnosis: 3 is odd and bigger than 2, so it agrees with the claim.
9 is odd and bigger than 2, so it agrees with the claim.
4 is not odd, so the claim says nothing about it.

questions.prompt: Goldbach's statement - every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes - has been checked up to 4 × 10¹⁸ but never proved. It is a...
questions.explanation: Believed, heavily tested, but unproved - a conjecture.

options.diagnosis: A theorem needs a proof. Huge evidence is still not a proof.
No counterexample has ever been found.

questions.prompt: Explain to a friend why checking a thousand examples does not prove a statement about all numbers, but one bad example can disprove it.
questions.explanation: Examples cannot cover infinitely many cases; one exception breaks an "every" claim.
rubric: There are infinitely many numbers, so examples can never cover them all.
A pattern can hold for many cases and then fail (or any similar point).
"Every" claims have no exceptions, so one failing case shows the claim is false.
questions.model_answer:
There are infinitely many numbers, so a thousand examples still leave infinitely many
unchecked - and patterns can break after many cases. A proof gives a reason that covers
every case at once. But a claim about every number has no room for exceptions, so finding
just one number where it fails is enough to show it is false.

connections_forward.how: Level 7 teaches the main methods of proof.
Counterexamples studied carefully.
How conjectures arise and how they are settled.
The Riemann Hypothesis is a conjecture - trillions of checked cases, but no proof.
Most experts conjecture that P is not equal to NP, but no one has a proof.

alternatives.title: The mathematician and the scientist
alternatives.text:
A scientist, an engineer and a mathematician are on a train through a new country. They see a
black sheep in a field. "Look," says the scientist, "the sheep here are black." The engineer
says, "At least one sheep here is black." The mathematician says, "There is at least one
field, containing at least one sheep, at least one side of which is black." The joke is about
the mathematician's care: claim exactly what you have shown, and nothing more. A proof is
what lets you claim more.

alternatives.title: Seeing why, not just that
alternatives.text:
Draw an even number of dots in two rows: every dot has a partner below or above it. Draw
another even number the same way. Slide the second drawing next to the first. The two rows
just get longer - every dot still has a partner. Notice that you never needed to know *which*
even numbers they were. A picture that works no matter which numbers you choose is a proof.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
Your friend says "every ball in this bag is red". You pull out three red balls. Is your
friend right? Maybe! But there might be a blue one at the bottom. If you pull out one blue
ball, you know for sure your friend was wrong. And the only way to know for sure they were
right is to have a good reason - like watching them fill the bag only from a box of red
balls. That good reason is what mathematicians call a proof.

l0-quantity.goal:
We are learning what a quantity is - "how many" or "how much" - and that it does not change
when things are moved around.
l0-quantity.why:
Mathematics studies quantities, not appearances. A row of coins spread out *looks* longer than
the same coins bunched up, but there are not more of them. Learning to see through
appearances to the quantity underneath is the first habit of mathematical thinking.
l0-quantity.problem: When two things look different, how do you know whether there is really more of one?
l0-quantity.plain:
A **quantity** is an amount: *how many* things there are, or *how much* of something there is.

- "How many" is for things you can count one by one: chairs, apples, people.
- "How much" is for things you measure rather than count: water, time, distance.

The important point: a quantity stays the same when you **rearrange** things. Spread out five
coins and you still have five coins. Pour juice into a taller glass and you still have the same
amount of juice. Only adding or taking away changes a quantity.

analogy.title: Juice in two glasses
analogy.text:
Pour a cup of juice into a tall thin glass, then into a short wide glass. In the tall glass
the juice reaches higher, so it *looks* like more. But you have not added or spilled a drop:
the quantity of juice is exactly the same. The shape of the container changed; the amount did
not.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: six cookies on a tray. The "Spread out" and "Bunch up" buttons move the
cookies around without adding or removing any. Watch the counter in the corner: it stays at 6
however the cookies are arranged.
visual.prompt: Spread the cookies out, bunch them up, then count them each time.

example_simple.title: Spread-out coins
example_simple.problem: Five coins are bunched together. Someone spreads them out in a long line. Are there more coins now?
steps: Spreading moves the coins; it does not add any.
Count them in the line - one, two, three, four, five.
example_simple.answer: No. There are still five coins - the quantity has not changed.

example_harder.title: How many, or how much?
example_harder.problem: Which of these are "how many" quantities, and which are "how much" quantities - the number of eggs in a box, the amount of milk in a jug, the length of a road, the number of pages in a book?
steps: Eggs and pages come in separate whole pieces you can count one at a time - these are "how many" quantities.
Milk and road length can be divided as finely as you like; you measure them instead of counting - these are "how much" quantities.
Both kinds are quantities, because both are amounts.
example_harder.answer: Eggs and pages are counted ("how many"). Milk and road length are measured ("how much").

word.text:
The mathematical word for an amount is **quantity**, from the Latin *quantus*, "how much".
Mathematicians sometimes call "how many" quantities *discrete* (made of separate pieces) and
"how much" quantities *continuous* (smoothly divisible). You do not need those words yet -
just the idea that both are amounts.

l0-quantity.no_symbol_note:
There is no single symbol for "quantity". Quantities are described by numbers, and number
symbols are introduced in [[lesson:l1-number-symbols|Number symbols]].

formal.statement:
A **quantity** is a property of a collection or object that can be counted or measured, and
that stays the same when the collection is rearranged or the object is moved or reshaped -
changing only when something is added or taken away.

glossary.meaning: A feature something has, such as its colour, its shape or its amount.
Found by counting one by one.
Found by comparing with a unit, such as a cup or a metre.
Moved into a different position or order, without adding or removing anything.

connections_back.how: Counting is how we find a "how many" quantity.

worked.title: The two rows of buttons
worked.problem: Row A has 6 buttons spaced far apart. Row B has 6 buttons squashed close together. A child says Row A has more. Is the child right, and how could you show them?
steps: Row A is longer, which is why it looks like more.
Match the buttons one-to-one - move each button of Row B next to a button of Row A.
Every button has exactly one partner, with none left over.
worked.answer: No - both rows have 6 buttons. Matching shows the quantities are equal even though the rows look different.

experiment.task: Make a tray of exactly 7 flowers. Then spread them out and bunch them up, checking the total each time.
experiment.success:
Moving the flowers never changed the total - only adding or removing did. Mathematics cares
about that unchanging amount, the quantity.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking a longer row must contain more objects.
mistakes.why: Length depends on spacing. Spreading things out changes how they look, not how many there are.
mistakes.fix: Count, or match one-to-one, instead of judging by eye.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking only countable things are quantities.
mistakes.why: Amounts of water, time or distance are quantities too - we measure them instead of counting.
mistakes.fix: Ask "is this an amount?" If yes, it is a quantity.

statements.text: Young children often judge a spread-out row of coins to contain more coins than the same coins bunched together.
statements.note: The psychologist Jean Piaget studied this; understanding that quantity survives rearrangement is called "conservation".

questions.prompt: Which of these are quantities? Choose all that apply.
questions.explanation: Pages, length and weight are amounts, so they are quantities. Colour and names are not amounts.

options.text: The number of pages in a book.
The weight of a bag of rice.

options.diagnosis: Colour is a property, but it is not an amount - you cannot count or measure "how much red".
A name is a label, not an amount.

questions.prompt: True or false: if you spread 8 coins out in a long line, there are more than 8 coins.
questions.explanation: False. Rearranging never changes a quantity.
questions.diagnosis: Spreading out changes the arrangement, not the quantity. Count them - still 8.

questions.prompt: The amount of water in a bath is a ...
questions.explanation: Water is measured, not counted, so it is a "how much" quantity.

options.text: "how many" quantity - we count it one by one.
options.diagnosis: Water does not come in separate pieces you can count; we measure it (for example in litres).
An amount of water is a quantity - it can be measured.

questions.prompt: Juice is poured from a short wide glass into a tall thin glass. Nothing is spilled. What happens to the amount of juice?
questions.explanation: The quantity of juice stays the same; only its shape changed.

options.text: It increases, because the juice is higher.
options.diagnosis: The juice is higher because the glass is thinner. Nothing was added, so the amount is unchanged.

options.text: It decreases, because the glass is thinner.
options.diagnosis: A thinner glass holds the same juice higher up. Nothing was removed.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what is a quantity, and what can and cannot change it?
questions.explanation: A quantity is an amount that survives rearrangement and changes only by adding or removing.
rubric: A quantity is an amount - how many or how much.
Rearranging, moving or reshaping does not change it.
Adding or taking away does change it.
questions.model_answer:
A quantity is an amount - how many things there are or how much of something there is.
Moving things around or pouring them into a different shape does not change it; only
adding some or taking some away does.

connections_forward.how: Measurement is how we find "how much" quantities.
Comparing tells us which of two quantities is bigger.
A number is the idea that names a quantity.

alternatives.title: The play-dough test
alternatives.text:
Roll a ball of play-dough (or bread dough, or clay). Now squash it flat into a pancake. Is
there more dough? Less? Roll it back into a ball - it is the same ball. The *shape* changed
completely, but the *amount* of dough never did. That unchanging amount is the quantity.

alternatives.title: Looks versus amount
alternatives.text:
Two things can look very different and have the same quantity:

- 5 coins in a heap and 5 coins in a long line - same quantity.
- A litre of water in a bucket and a litre in a bottle - same quantity.

And two things can look similar and have different quantities:

- A full glass and a glass with one sip taken - looks almost the same, but a little less.

Mathematics trains you to ask "how much is really there?" rather than "how does it look?"

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
If you have 4 sweets in your hand and you open your fingers so they spread out, do you have
more sweets? No! Still 4. The only way to get more sweets is for someone to give you one, and
the only way to have fewer is to eat one. "How many sweets" is a quantity. Moving them around
does not change it.

l0-real-world.goal:
We are learning how mathematics describes real situations using models - and why every model
leaves something out.
l0-real-world.why:
Mathematics is powerful in the real world because we can describe a situation with numbers and
rules, then *reason* about it to make predictions. Weather forecasts, bridges and phone networks
all rely on mathematical models. Knowing what models can and cannot do is part of thinking like a
mathematician.
l0-real-world.problem:
How can thinking about numbers and rules tell you anything about the real world - about money,
journeys, or how much paint to buy?
l0-real-world.plain:
To use mathematics on a real situation, we build a **model**:

1. **Pick out the quantities that matter** - money saved, distance walked, tiles needed.
2. **Describe how they are connected with a rule** - "I add 5 coins every week".
3. **Reason with the rule** to make a prediction - "after 4 weeks I will have added 20 coins".
4. **Check the prediction against reality**, and improve the model if needed.

A model is always **simpler than reality**. A savings model ignores the week you forget to save;
a walking model ignores getting tired. That is not a flaw - leaving out details is what makes the
model useful. But it means a model's predictions are only as good as its assumptions.

analogy.title: A map is a model
analogy.text:
A map of a city leaves out almost everything - trees, people, the colour of doors - and keeps
only what you need to find your way: streets and their connections. Because it leaves so much
out, it fits in your pocket. A mathematical model is a map of a situation, drawn with numbers
and rules.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a savings jar described by a model. The model has two numbers - how many
coins are in the jar at the start, and how many are added each week - and one rule: "each week,
add the weekly amount". The slider moves forward in time, and the model predicts how many coins
the jar holds after each week.
visual.prompt: Change the starting amount and the weekly amount, and predict the total before moving the slider.

example_simple.title: The savings jar
example_simple.problem: A jar has 10 coins. You add 5 coins every week. How many coins after 2 weeks?
steps: The quantities that matter - coins in the jar, and coins added per week.
The rule - each week, add 5.
After week 1 - 10 and 5 more is 15.
After week 2 - 15 and 5 more is 20.
example_simple.answer: 20 coins - if you really do save 5 every week.

example_harder.title: The walking model
example_harder.problem: A walker covers 3 kilometres every hour. The model predicts 12 kilometres after 4 hours. In reality she covers only 10. Was the mathematics wrong?
steps: The arithmetic was right - 3 kilometres each hour for 4 hours is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.
The model assumed she walks at exactly the same speed for 4 hours.
Real walkers get tired, stop for water and walk uphill. The model left those details out.
The mismatch tells us the model's assumption was too simple, not that the arithmetic failed. A better model might include a rest.
example_harder.answer: The reasoning was correct, but the model was too simple. Prediction errors usually point to missing details in the model.

word.text:
A simplified description of a real situation in numbers and rules is called a **mathematical
model**. The things a model takes for granted - "she walks at the same speed" - are its
**assumptions**.

l0-real-world.no_symbol_note:
Models are written with symbols, and in Level 4 you will see how letters let a model describe
quantities that change - see [[lesson:l4-why-letters|Why letters appear in mathematics]]. For now,
words and numbers are enough.

formal.statement:
A **mathematical model** is a simplified representation of a real-world situation in which the
relevant quantities are represented by numbers and the relationships between them by
mathematical rules. Conclusions drawn from a model hold for the real situation only to the
extent that the model's assumptions are accurate.

glossary.meaning: A description that keeps the important parts and leaves out the rest.
The amounts that matter for the question being asked.
How the quantities depend on one another.
What the model takes for granted about the situation.

notation.read_aloud: ten plus five plus five plus five plus five equals thirty

parts.meaning: The coins in the jar at the start.
The coins added each week - four times, for four weeks.
The predicted total after four weeks.

notation.english: Starting with 10 coins and adding 5 each week for four weeks gives 30 coins.

connections_back.how: Models need quantities, and many quantities come from measuring.
The heart of a model is a rule connecting quantities.
Symbols let us write models compactly.

worked.title: Tiling a floor
worked.problem: A floor is to be covered with square tiles - 4 rows, each with 6 tiles. How many tiles are needed? What might the model leave out?
steps: The quantities - rows (4), tiles per row (6), total tiles.
The rule - the total is 4 rows of 6, counted row by row - 6, 12, 18, 24.
The model predicts 24 tiles.
What it leaves out - tiles break when cut, rooms are not perfect rectangles, a builder buys spares.
worked.answer: 24 tiles in the model. A sensible builder buys a few extra, because the model assumes no breakages.

experiment.task: Use the journey model to predict how far a traveller goes in 5 hours. Make your prediction before moving the slider, then check it.
experiment.success:
Your prediction came from reasoning with the model's rule, not from watching the journey.
That is what models are for - and checking against reality is how we find out whether the
model's assumptions were good ones.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking a model's prediction is guaranteed to come true.
mistakes.why: A model is only as good as its assumptions. Reality has details the model left out.
mistakes.fix: Treat predictions as "what happens if the assumptions hold", and check them.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking a wrong prediction means the arithmetic was wrong.
mistakes.why: Often the arithmetic is fine and an assumption is wrong.
mistakes.fix: When a model fails, look first at what it assumed.

mistakes.mistake: Trying to put every detail into a model.
mistakes.why: A model with everything in it is as complicated as reality, and no longer useful.
mistakes.fix: Keep only the details that matter for your question.

statements.text: Weather forecasts are computed from mathematical models of the atmosphere.
"All models are wrong, but some are useful" is a saying attributed to the statistician George Box.
statements.note: It means every model simplifies, but a good simplification can still predict well.

questions.prompt: A jar has 10 coins. You add 5 coins each week. According to the model, how many coins are in the jar after 3 weeks?
questions.explanation: 10, then 15 after week 1, 20 after week 2, 25 after week 3.

common_wrong.diagnosis: That is the coins added over 3 weeks. Do not forget the 10 that were in the jar at the start.
That is after 2 weeks. Add one more week of 5 coins.

questions.prompt: A model says a plant grows 2 cm every day. Which real detail does this model leave out?
questions.explanation: The model assumes the same growth every day, ignoring weather and other changes.

options.text: Plants grow at different speeds in cold weather.
The plant gets taller as days pass.
options.diagnosis: The model includes that - it is exactly what "grows 2 cm every day" describes.
The model includes the unit - centimetres.

questions.prompt: True or false: if a model's prediction turns out wrong, there must be a mistake in the arithmetic.
questions.explanation: False. Usually an assumption, not the arithmetic, is to blame.
questions.diagnosis: The arithmetic can be perfect while an assumption of the model is unrealistic.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a mathematical model?
questions.explanation: The timetable rule describes quantities (times) with a rule, so we can predict.

options.text: "A bus leaves every 15 minutes, starting at 8:00" - used to predict when buses arrive.
A photograph of a bus stop.
options.diagnosis: A photograph shows the situation but gives no quantities or rules to reason with.
A poem may describe buses, but it does not give quantities and rules for prediction.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what is a mathematical model, and why can its predictions be wrong?
questions.explanation: Models describe situations with numbers and rules; they simplify, so predictions depend on assumptions.
rubric: A model describes a real situation using numbers and rules.
It is used to make predictions.
It is simpler than reality / leaves details out, so its assumptions may not hold.
questions.model_answer:
A mathematical model describes a real situation with numbers and rules so we can reason about
it and make predictions. It is always simpler than reality - it leaves details out - so if an
assumption does not hold, the prediction can be wrong even though the reasoning was right.

connections_forward.how: Level 1 looks closely at the numbers that models are built from.
Letters let models describe quantities that change.
Mathematicians model the primes as if they were random - a model that makes remarkably good predictions, and that the Riemann Hypothesis helps to justify.

alternatives.title: Packing for a trip
alternatives.text:
