Planning a 5-day trip, you think: "I need 1 shirt per day, plus 1 spare - so 6 shirts." That
is a model! The quantities are days and shirts; the rule is "one per day, plus a spare". It
ignores the possibility of spilling soup on two shirts in one day - and that is fine,
because the spare covers most surprises. Everyday planning is full of small mathematical
models.

alternatives.title: What does the model assume?
alternatives.text:
For each model, ask "what is it assuming?"

- "A car at 60 km per hour travels 120 km in 2 hours." Assumes: no traffic, no stops.
- "A class of 30 needs 30 chairs." Assumes: everyone comes, nobody brings a friend.
- "A pizza for every 3 people." Assumes: everyone is equally hungry.

Finding the assumptions is the most important skill in using mathematics on the real world.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
If you eat 2 biscuits every day, how many biscuits do you need for 3 days? 2, 4, 6 - six
biscuits! That is a little model: it pretends you always eat exactly 2. On a hungry day you
might eat 3 - then the model is a bit wrong. Models are guesses about the world that use
numbers, and they work well when the world behaves the way we pretended.

l0-reasoning.goal:
We are learning what mathematical reasoning is: reaching conclusions that *must* be true
because of facts we already know.
l0-reasoning.why:
Reasoning is what makes mathematics different from guessing. A pattern suggests; reasoning
guarantees. Every proof, including any future proof about prime numbers or computation, is a
chain of reasoning steps.
l0-reasoning.problem: How can you know something for certain without checking it directly?
l0-reasoning.plain:
**Reasoning** means starting from facts you are sure of, and working out new facts that
**must** follow.

Here is a tiny example. Suppose you know two things:

- Every cat has whiskers.
- Tom is a cat.

Then you can be completely sure that Tom has whiskers - without ever seeing Tom.

Notice the difference from patterns. "The sun has risen every day I remember, so it will rise
tomorrow" is a reasonable *guess* from a pattern. But "every cat has whiskers, Tom is a cat, so
Tom has whiskers" is not a guess - if the starting facts are true, the conclusion *cannot* be
false.

Reasoning can also go wrong. "Every cat has four legs, my dog has four legs, so my dog is a
cat" sounds similar, but the conclusion does not follow - plenty of four-legged things are not
cats. Learning to tell good reasoning from bad is a central skill in mathematics.

analogy.title: The detective
analogy.text:
A detective knows the thief left the house before 9 o'clock, and knows that Sam was at the
house until 10 o'clock. The detective concludes that Sam is not the thief - without fingerprints,
without a confession, purely by reasoning. If both facts are true, the conclusion must be true.
Mathematicians are detectives whose clues are definitions and proven facts.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: three bags labelled A, B and C. Their weights are hidden. You can put any
two bags on the balance, and it tips toward the heavier one. Every weighing is recorded as a
fact. The panel on the right shows what can be *concluded* from those facts - including
comparisons you never made directly.
visual.prompt: Find the order of the three bags from heaviest to lightest using as few weighings as you can.

example_simple.title: Whiskers
example_simple.problem: Facts - every cat has whiskers; Tom is a cat. What can you conclude?
steps: The first fact is about *every* cat, with no exceptions.
The second fact says Tom is one of those cats.
So whatever is true of every cat is true of Tom.
example_simple.answer: Tom has whiskers. This conclusion must be true if the two facts are.

example_harder.title: A chain of weighings
example_harder.problem: Bag A is heavier than bag B. Bag B is heavier than bag C. You never weighed A against C. Which is heavier?
steps: A outweighs B, so A is heavier than B.
B outweighs C, so B is heavier than C.
Anything heavier than B is heavier than everything B is heavier than - so A is heavier than C.
We reached a fact about A and C without ever comparing them directly.
example_harder.answer: A is heavier than C, and the full order is A, B, C. Reasoning gave us a fact we never measured.

word.text:
This is **reasoning** (more fully, *logical reasoning*). The facts you start from are sometimes
called **premises**, and the new fact you reach is the **conclusion**. Reasoning in mathematics
usually starts from **definitions** - exact statements of what words mean - and from facts that
have already been proved.

symbols.name: therefore sign
symbols.looks_like: Three dots arranged in a triangle, pointing upward.
symbols.means: "Therefore" - what comes next follows from what came before.
symbols.why: It is a quick way to mark the conclusion of a piece of reasoning.

formal.statement:
**Mathematical reasoning** is the process of deriving new statements from accepted facts,
definitions and assumptions, in such a way that each new statement follows necessarily from
statements already established. A conclusion reached this way is guaranteed to be true
whenever the starting facts are true.

glossary.meaning: Obtaining by careful steps.
A sentence that is either true or false.
Facts already known to be true, or agreed as starting points.
Cannot be false if the earlier statements are true.

notation.expression: A \text{ heavier than } B,\quad B \text{ heavier than } C \quad\therefore\quad A \text{ heavier than } C
notation.read_aloud: A is heavier than B, and B is heavier than C, therefore A is heavier than C

parts.meaning: Separates the two facts we start from.

notation.english: From two weighings, we know a third comparison without doing it.

connections_back.how: Reasoning follows exact steps, just as a rule does.
Chains of comparisons are one of the simplest kinds of reasoning.

worked.title: Spot the bad argument
worked.problem: "All birds have feathers. My pillow has feathers. Therefore my pillow is a bird." What is wrong?
steps: The first fact says every bird has feathers. It does *not* say that only birds have feathers.
The pillow having feathers does not make it one of the birds.
The conclusion does not follow, even though both starting facts are true.
worked.answer: The reasoning is faulty. Knowing all birds have feathers tells you nothing about which feathered things are birds.

experiment.task: There are four bags this time. Work out the complete order from heaviest to lightest, letting reasoning fill in the comparisons you do not make.
experiment.success:
You never compared every pair, yet you know the whole order. The extra knowledge came from
reasoning, not from the balance. That is the power of reasoning: it multiplies what you know.

mistakes.mistake: Treating a pattern as if it were reasoning.
mistakes.why: A pattern seen many times is still a guess about the next case; reasoning guarantees it.
mistakes.fix: Ask, "must this be true, or has it just been true so far?"

mistakes.mistake: Reversing a fact ("all cats have whiskers, so everything with whiskers is a cat").
mistakes.why: "All A are B" does not mean "all B are A". Dogs have whiskers too.
mistakes.fix: Check which way round the fact goes.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming the conclusion is true just because the reasoning looks tidy.
mistakes.why: If a starting fact is false, the conclusion can be false even with perfect reasoning.
mistakes.fix: Check both the starting facts and each step.

statements.text: If A is heavier than B and B is heavier than C, then A is heavier than C.
statements.note: This property of "heavier than" is called transitivity. Many comparisons - taller, older, greater - have it.

questions.prompt: Facts - every square has four corners; this shape is a square. What must be true?
questions.explanation: Whatever is true of every square is true of this square.

options.text: Every shape with four corners is a square.
options.diagnosis: That reverses the fact. Rectangles have four corners too but are not all squares.
The two facts together guarantee the shape has four corners.

questions.prompt: Which argument is faulty?
questions.explanation: Living in water does not make something a fish - whales are mammals. The fact "all fish live in water" cannot be reversed.

options.text: All fish live in water. A whale lives in water. Therefore a whale is a fish.
All fish live in water. A trout is a fish. Therefore a trout lives in water.
options.diagnosis: This one is sound - the trout is one of the fish, so it lives in water.

questions.prompt: True or false: if the starting facts are true and every step of reasoning is correct, the conclusion must be true.
questions.explanation: True. That guarantee is the point of reasoning.
questions.diagnosis: That is exactly what makes reasoning reliable - correct steps from true facts cannot lead to a false conclusion.

questions.prompt: Ali is taller than Ben. Ben is taller than Cara. Who is the shortest?
questions.explanation: Ali is taller than Ben, who is taller than Cara, so Cara is the shortest.

options.diagnosis: Ben is taller than Cara, so Ben is not the shortest.
Ali is taller than Ben, who is taller than Cara - Ali is the tallest.
The two facts chain together - Ali, then Ben, then Cara.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between guessing from a pattern and reasoning. Give an example of each.
questions.explanation: Patterns suggest; reasoning guarantees.
rubric: A pattern only shows what has happened so far; the next case could differ.
Reasoning gives a conclusion that must be true if the starting facts are true.
Gives a sensible example of each.
questions.model_answer:
A pattern only tells you what has happened so far - "it rained the last three Mondays" does
not make next Monday rainy. Reasoning gives conclusions that must be true if the starting
facts are - "every cat has whiskers and Tom is a cat, so Tom has whiskers" cannot be wrong
if the facts are right.

connections_forward.how: A proof is a complete chain of reasoning that settles a question for every case.
Level 7 makes logical arguments precise.
Common ways reasoning goes wrong, studied carefully.

alternatives.title: Three cups
alternatives.text:
Fill three cups with different amounts of water and label them A, B and C. Pour to compare
only A with B and then only B with C (hold them up side by side). Suppose A has more than B
and B has more than C. Before comparing A and C, say out loud which has more. Then check.
You were right *before* you looked - because the conclusion followed from what you already
knew. That is reasoning.

alternatives.title: Must versus probably
alternatives.text:
Sort these into "must be true" and "probably true":

- "Every number in my list is even. 14 is in my list. So 14 is even." - **must**.
- "The last five buses were late. So the next bus will be late." - **probably** (a pattern).
- "A is older than B, B is older than C. So A is older than C." - **must**.

Reasoning lives in the "must" column.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
All the toys in the red box are cars. You pull a toy out of the red box. What is it? A car!
You didn't even look - you just knew. Knowing something for sure because of other things you
know is called reasoning.

l0-rules.goal:
We are learning what a mathematical rule is: an exact instruction that always turns the same
starting point into the same result.
l0-rules.why:
Patterns are produced by rules. Rules are also the seed of two huge ideas: *functions*
(rules that turn inputs into outputs) and *algorithms* (rules written as exact steps a
computer can follow) - and algorithms are what P versus NP is about.
l0-rules.problem:
How can an instruction be made so precise that everyone who follows it gets exactly the same
answer?
l0-rules.plain:
A **rule** is an instruction that tells you exactly what to do with something - and always gives
the same result when you start from the same thing.

"Double the number" is a rule. Give it 3 and it gives back 6. Give it 3 again tomorrow and it
still gives 6.

A good rule must be **exact**: there must be no choices left to the person following it.
"Pick a bigger number" is not a mathematical rule, because two people could pick differently.

Rules can be **combined**: "double it, then add one" is a rule made of two steps, done in a
fixed order.

Finally, a surprising fact: seeing a few results does not tell you the rule for certain.
If a rule turns 1 into 2 and 2 into 4, it might be "double it" (so 3 becomes 6) - but it could
just as well be a different rule that turns 3 into 5. You need more evidence, or to be told
the rule.

analogy.title: The vending machine
analogy.text:
Press B4 on a vending machine and out comes the same snack every time. The machine follows a
rule: each button produces one particular snack. It never thinks "I'll give a different one
today". Mathematical rules are perfectly reliable machines like that - except they work on
numbers, shapes and other mathematical objects.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a machine with a slot on the left where you put a number in, and a slot
on the right where a number comes out. The label shows the rule the machine follows. A table
underneath records every number you have put in and what came out.
visual.prompt: Put in several numbers. Then put in the same number twice and check you get the same result.

example_simple.title: Add three
example_simple.problem: A rule says "add 3". What comes out when you put in 4?
steps: The rule tells you exactly what to do - count on 3 from 4.
Five, six, seven.

example_harder.title: Finding a hidden rule
example_harder.problem: A hidden rule turns 1 into 3, 2 into 5, and 3 into 7. What does it turn 10 into?
steps: The outputs 3, 5, 7 go up by 2 each time the input goes up by 1.
Going up by 2 for each step suggests "double it" is involved. Doubling gives 2, 4, 6 - each one less than the outputs.
So the rule seems to be "double it, then add 1" - check - 1 gives 3, 2 gives 5, 3 gives 7. It fits every example.
Applying it to 10 - double 10 is 20, add 1 gives 21.
example_harder.answer: 21 - if the rule really is "double, then add 1". Three examples fit, but only being told the rule would make us certain.

word.text:
The word is **rule**. The thing you start with is often called the **input** and the result the
**output**. Later in the course, a rule that gives exactly one output for every input will be
called a **function** - but that is a story for Level 4.

symbols.name: maps-to arrow
symbols.looks_like: An arrow pointing right, with a small upright bar at its tail.
symbols.means: "Goes to" or "is turned into" by a rule. $3 \mapsto 6$ means "3 is turned into 6".
symbols.why: It shows a single step of a rule compactly, without writing a sentence.
symbols.read_aloud: "Maps to" or "goes to" - so $3 \mapsto 6$ is "three maps to six".

formal.statement:
A **rule** is a precise procedure that assigns to each allowed input exactly one output. Applying
a rule to the same input always produces the same output.

glossary.meaning: Exact instructions with no choices left open.
Gives or attaches.
Something the rule is designed to work on - for example, a number.
One result - never none, never several.

notation.read_aloud: three maps to six
notation.english: Following the rule, 3 becomes 6 (for example, the rule "double it").

connections_back.how: Patterns are produced by rules - the rule explains why the pattern continues.

worked.title: Two rules, same start
worked.problem: Rule A is "double it". Rule B is "if the input is 1, add 1; otherwise, add 2". Do these rules agree?
steps: Rule A turns 1 into 2, 2 into 4 and 3 into 6.
Rule B turns 1 into 2 (it adds 1), 2 into 4 (it adds 2) and 3 into 5 (it adds 2).
Both rules agree on the inputs 1 and 2, but give different outputs for 3.
So knowing that 1 goes to 2 and 2 goes to 4 is not enough to know what 3 goes to.
worked.answer: Only partly - they agree on 1 and 2 but disagree on 3. Two different rules can agree on some inputs and differ on others, so a few examples never pin a rule down completely.

experiment.task: This machine's rule is hidden. Feed it numbers, watch the outputs, and work out the rule.
experiment.success:
You found the rule by experimenting and looking for a pattern in the outputs. This is how much
of mathematics begins - experiment, notice, guess - before anyone writes a proof.

mistakes.mistake: Accepting a vague instruction as a rule ("make it bigger").
mistakes.why: Different people would get different results, so it is not exact.
mistakes.fix: A rule must say *exactly* what to do - "add 3", "double it".

mistakes.mistake: Doing the steps of a combined rule in the wrong order.
mistakes.why: "Double, then add 1" turns 5 into 11. "Add 1, then double" turns 5 into 12. Order matters.
mistakes.fix: Follow the steps in the order they are written.

mistakes.mistake: Being certain of a hidden rule after one or two examples.
mistakes.why: Many different rules fit a few examples.
mistakes.fix: Test your guess on more inputs, and remember it is still a guess until confirmed.

statements.text: Any finite list of examples fits more than one rule - for instance, 1 to 2 and 2 to 4 fits both "double it" and many other rules.

questions.prompt: The rule is "double it". What does 7 turn into?
questions.explanation: Two lots of 7 is 14.

common_wrong.diagnosis: That adds 2. Doubling means taking two lots of the number - 7 and 7 more.

questions.prompt: A hidden rule turns 1 into 4, 2 into 5 and 3 into 6. If the rule is the simplest one that fits, what does it turn 10 into?
questions.hint: How much bigger is each output than its input?
questions.explanation: Each output is 3 more than its input, so the rule is "add 3" and 10 becomes 13.

common_wrong.diagnosis: The rule is applied to the input you put in - 10 - not to the last output.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a mathematical rule?
questions.explanation: "Add 5" is exact - every input has exactly one output.

options.text: Choose any number bigger than the one you were given.
options.diagnosis: This leaves a choice, so two people could get different results.
This is not exact - there is no single result.

questions.prompt: True or false: a mathematical rule can give different outputs for the same input on different days.
questions.explanation: False. The same input always produces the same output.
questions.diagnosis: A rule always gives the same output for the same input - that is what makes it a rule.

questions.prompt: The rule is "add 1, then double". What does 5 turn into?
questions.explanation: Add 1 to get 6, then double to get 12.

common_wrong.diagnosis: That doubles first and adds 1 second. This rule adds 1 first, then doubles.

questions.prompt: A rule turns 1 into 2 and 2 into 4. Explain why you cannot be completely sure what it turns 3 into.
questions.explanation: Several rules fit any few examples, so the examples alone do not decide the next output.
rubric: Different rules can produce the same outputs for 1 and 2.
Gives or describes two possibilities for 3 (for example 6 by doubling, or something else).
Knowing a few examples does not determine the rule; you need the rule itself or more evidence.
questions.model_answer:
Lots of different rules turn 1 into 2 and 2 into 4. "Double it" would turn 3 into 6, but
another rule could agree on 1 and 2 and still turn 3 into 5. A few examples cannot pin the
rule down - you would need to be told the rule, or test many more inputs.

connections_forward.how: Following rules exactly is the beginning of logical reasoning.
A rule from inputs to outputs is called a function.
An algorithm is a rule written as exact steps - the subject of P versus NP.

alternatives.title: A recipe card
alternatives.text:
A recipe is a rule for cooks: "Take 2 eggs, add 100 g of flour, mix, bake for 20 minutes."
Follow it exactly and you get the same cake each time. If a recipe said "add some flour",
different cooks would get different cakes - that is not a precise rule. Mathematical rules
are like perfect recipes: every step exact, so the result is always the same.

alternatives.title: Be the machine
alternatives.text:
Pretend you are a machine with the rule "times ten".

- Someone gives you 4. What do you hand back? (40)
- Someone gives you 4 again. What now? (Still 40 - a machine does not change its mind.)
- Someone gives you 0. What now? (0)

Now be a machine with the rule "think of a bigger number". Someone gives you 4 - what do
you hand back? You have to *choose*. A real mathematical rule never asks you to choose.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
Imagine a magic box. When you put one toy in, two toys come out! Put in two, four come out!
The box always does exactly the same thing - it doubles. That "always the same" instruction
is a rule. If the box gave you a different number of toys every time, it would not have a
rule - it would just be a surprise box.

l0-symbols.goal: We are learning why mathematics uses symbols, and how to read our first two: $+$ and $=$.
l0-symbols.why:
Mathematical writing can look frightening - a wall of strange marks. But every symbol is just a
short name for an idea you can understand in words. Knowing *why* symbols exist turns them from
a barrier into a convenience.
l0-symbols.problem:
Mathematical ideas described only in words become long, slow and easy to misread. How can we
write them quickly, exactly, and in a way any reader in any country understands?
l0-symbols.plain:
A **symbol** is a short mark that stands for an idea. Mathematics uses symbols for three reasons:

1. **They are short.** "Three added to four is the same amount as seven" becomes $3 + 4 = 7$.
2. **They are exact.** A symbol means one agreed thing, with none of the vagueness of everyday words.
3. **They are shared.** A French, a Chinese and an Arabic speaker all read $3 + 4 = 7$ the same way,
   though they would say it with completely different words.

There is a fourth, deeper reason: once ideas are written compactly, you can *work* with them -
rearrange them, spot patterns in them, and reason with them - far more easily than with long
sentences.

Every symbol you will ever meet in this course will be introduced only after you understand the
idea it stands for. Symbols are names, not mysteries.

analogy.title: Road signs
analogy.text:
A road sign with a picture of a bicycle inside a red circle means "no cycling" in many countries,
whatever language you speak. Drivers read it in a fraction of a second. Mathematical symbols do
the same job for ideas: short, exact, and understood across languages.

statements.words: three added to four is the same amount as seven
ten is the same amount as five added to five
one added to one added to one is the same amount as three

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: sentences written two ways - in ordinary English on the left, and in
mathematical symbols on the right. Tap a sentence to switch between its two forms. The meaning is
identical; only the writing changes.
visual.prompt: Tap each sentence to see it in symbols. Which version is quicker to read?

example_simple.title: Into symbols
example_simple.problem: Write "five added to two is the same amount as seven" in symbols.
steps: "Five" becomes 5, "two" becomes 2 and "seven" becomes 7.
"Added to" becomes the plus sign $+$.
"Is the same amount as" becomes the equals sign $=$.

example_harder.title: A long sentence made short
example_harder.problem: An old arithmetic book might say - "If you take some number, double it, and then add three, you obtain eleven." How much shorter can this become?
steps: We do not know the number yet, so put an empty box in its place - $\square$.
"Double it" means two of that number - written $2 \times \square$ (you will meet $\times$ in Level 1).
"Then add three" becomes $+\;3$, and "you obtain eleven" becomes $=\;11$.
The whole sentence becomes $2 \times \square + 3 = 11$.
example_harder.answer: Twenty words become a handful of symbols. In Level 4 the box will be replaced by a letter, and you will learn to find the hidden number.

word.text:
A mark that stands for an idea is called a **symbol**. A line of symbols that says something
complete, like $3 + 4 = 7$, is often called a **mathematical sentence** or **statement**.

symbols.name: plus sign
symbols.looks_like: A small upright cross - one horizontal stroke and one vertical stroke.
symbols.means: "Added to", "and", "put together with". $3 + 4$ means three put together with four.
symbols.why: Writing "and" or "added to" over and over was slow. The cross first appeared in print in a German arithmetic book in 1489, and possibly grew out of a quick way of writing the Latin word *et*, meaning "and".

symbols.name: equals sign
symbols.looks_like: Two short horizontal lines, one above the other, the same length.
symbols.means: "Is the same amount as". It says the thing on the left and the thing on the right are equal.
symbols.why: Robert Recorde invented it in 1557, writing that he chose two parallel lines "bicause noe .2. thynges, can be moare equalle".
symbols.read_aloud: "Equals" or "is equal to" - so $3 + 4 = 7$ is "three plus four equals seven".

formal.statement:
A **mathematical symbol** is a written sign that, by agreed convention, stands for a specific
mathematical object (such as a number), operation (such as adding) or relation (such as
equality).

glossary.meaning: A mark on paper or screen.
Everyone has agreed what it means - the meaning is shared, not personal.
A thing mathematics talks about, such as a number or a shape.
Something you do to objects, such as adding them.
A way two objects can be connected, such as "is equal to".

notation.read_aloud: three plus four equals seven
notation.english: Three and four put together make exactly the same amount as seven.

connections_back.how: The digits 3, 4 and 7 are symbols for counting words.
Rules become much easier to state once we have symbols.

worked.title: Reading aloud
worked.problem: Read $8 = 3 + 5$ aloud, and say what it means.
steps: Read left to right, one symbol at a time - "eight", "equals", "three", "plus", "five".
Notice the answer is on the left this time. That is fine - $=$ only says the two sides are the same amount.
Meaning - eight is the same amount as three and five put together.
worked.answer: "Eight equals three plus five" - eight is the same amount as three and five together.

statements.words: two added to two is the same amount as four
six is the same amount as one added to five
nine added to zero is the same amount as nine
four added to three is the same amount as three added to four

experiment.task: Before revealing each symbolic version, try to write it yourself. Then reveal all four.
experiment.success:
Notice the last one, $4 + 3 = 3 + 4$. Neither side is "the answer" - the equals sign just says
the two sides are the same amount. Keeping that meaning in mind will make algebra much easier.

mistakes.mistake: Reading "=" as "here comes the answer".
mistakes.why: Then $8 = 3 + 5$ or $4 + 3 = 3 + 4$ look wrong, though both are true. The equals sign is a statement that two things are the same amount.
mistakes.fix: Read $=$ as "is the same amount as", every time.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking symbols are a separate, secret language.
mistakes.why: Every symbol abbreviates an idea that can be said in ordinary words.
mistakes.fix: When you meet a symbol, ask, "how would I say this in words?"

statements.text: The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde in his 1557 book *The Whetstone of Witte*.
The plus sign first appeared in print in a German arithmetic book by Johannes Widmann in 1489.
The shape of a symbol is a matter of agreement. What matters is that everyone uses it the same way.

questions.prompt: Why does mathematics use symbols? Choose all that apply.
questions.explanation: Symbols are short, exact and shared across languages.

options.text: They make ideas quick to write and read.
They are understood by readers of many different languages.
To keep mathematics secret from ordinary people.
options.diagnosis: Symbols are abbreviations for ideas that can always be explained in words - they make mathematics easier to share, not harder.

questions.prompt: Write "six added to three is the same amount as nine" in symbols.
questions.hint: Use 6, 3, 9, the plus sign and the equals sign.

questions.prompt: True or false: the equals sign means "here comes the answer".
questions.explanation: False. It means "is the same amount as".
questions.diagnosis: "=" says both sides are the same amount. $7 = 3 + 4$ and $3 + 4 = 4 + 3$ are both true.

questions.prompt: How do you read $10 = 6 + 4$ aloud?
questions.explanation: Reading left to right - "ten equals six plus four".

options.diagnosis: Read the symbols in order - the plus sign sits between 6 and 4.

options.text: This cannot be read, because the answer is on the wrong side.
options.diagnosis: There is no wrong side. "=" just says both sides are the same amount.

questions.prompt: True or false: $5 + 2 = 2 + 5$ is a true statement.
questions.explanation: True. Both sides equal 7.
questions.diagnosis: Both sides make seven, so they are the same amount.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words what a mathematical symbol is, using $=$ as an example.
questions.explanation: A symbol is an agreed short name for an idea; $=$ means "is the same amount as".
rubric: A symbol is a short mark that stands for an idea.
Its meaning is agreed, so everyone reads it the same way.
Correctly explains that $=$ means "is the same amount as".
questions.model_answer:
A symbol is a short mark that stands for an idea, with a meaning everyone has agreed on.
For example, $=$ stands for "is the same amount as" - so $3 + 4 = 7$ says three and four
together are the same amount as seven.

connections_forward.how: The symbols for numbers - digits and place value.
What "equal" really means.
Level 3 is entirely about reading mathematical symbols.
Letters are symbols for numbers we do not know yet.

alternatives.title: Music notation
alternatives.text:
A musician reading sheet music sees dots on lines and instantly knows which note to play, how
long to hold it and how loud. Writing the same information in words - "play the note A for
half a beat, fairly softly" - would fill pages. Musical symbols were invented because words
were too slow. Mathematical symbols were invented for exactly the same reason.

alternatives.title: Before symbols
alternatives.text:
For most of history, mathematics was written entirely in words. A problem might read "a
quantity, and its double, and three more, together make twenty-four". Mathematicians spent
enormous effort just *reading* their own problems. Between the 1400s and 1600s, European
writers gradually introduced the symbols $+$, $-$ and $=$, and later letters for unknown
numbers. Once problems became short enough to see at a glance, mathematics sped up
dramatically. Symbols did not make mathematics harder - they made modern mathematics
possible.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
Instead of saying "I have three sweets and you give me two more sweets and now I have five
sweets", we can write a tiny secret code that is not really secret at all: $3 + 2 = 5$. The
little cross means "and some more", and the two lines mean "makes the same as". It is just a
quick way of writing the same thing.

l0-what-is-mathematics.goal: We are learning what mathematics actually is - and what it is not.
l0-what-is-mathematics.why:
Many people think mathematics *means* doing sums. Sums are only a small part of it.
If you know what mathematics really studies, every later idea - numbers, symbols,
equations, proofs - has a place to fit, and nothing feels like a random rule to memorise.
l0-what-is-mathematics.problem:
It answers the question "What kind of thinking is this, and why would anyone do it?"
so that the rest of the journey has a purpose.
l0-what-is-mathematics.plain:
Mathematics is a way of thinking very carefully about a few kinds of question:

- **How many? How much?** - counting and measuring.
- **What comes next?** - noticing things that repeat or grow regularly.
- **What shape? How is it built?** - the way things are arranged and connected.
- **What must be true?** - working out facts that cannot be otherwise.

Mathematics is also a *language*. Ordinary language is wonderful for stories and feelings, but
it is often vague: "a few", "quite big", "soon". Mathematics is a language where every
sentence means exactly one thing, so people can agree completely on whether it is right.

Doing sums is a small part of mathematics, in the way that spelling words is a small part of
writing a novel.

analogy.title: A new language, learned like a child learns to talk
analogy.text:
A child learning to speak first understands *things* - a ball, a cup, "more!" - and only later
learns the words, and later still the grammar. Mathematics can be learned the same way.
In this course every idea comes first as something you can see and touch, then gets its word,
then its symbol, and only then its exact definition. You will never be asked to use a word
you have not been taught.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a staircase made of square blocks - 1 block, then 2, then 3, then 4.
The buttons are four "lenses". Each lens shows a different kind of mathematical thinking about
the *same* staircase: how many blocks (quantity), how the steps grow (pattern), what shape it
makes (structure), and what we can be sure of without building it (reasoning).
visual.prompt: Switch between the four lenses, then add a step and watch every lens update.

example_simple.title: Counting apples
example_simple.problem: You count the apples in a bowl and find there are 6. Was that mathematics?
steps: You were answering the question "how many?" - a question about **quantity**.
You said one counting word for each apple, in order. That is a precise method.
Anyone else who counts carefully will also get 6. Mathematics gives answers everyone can agree on.
example_simple.answer: Yes. Counting is one of the simplest pieces of mathematics - it deals with quantity.

example_harder.title: Sharing sweets fairly
example_harder.problem: Twelve sweets are to be shared fairly between some friends. What kinds of mathematical thinking does this involve?
steps: **Quantity**: there are 12 sweets.
**Structure**: "fairly" means everyone gets the same amount - we are arranging 12 things into equal groups.
**Pattern**: with 2 friends each gets 6, with 3 each gets 4, with 4 each gets 3... There is a regular connection between the number of friends and the share.
**Reasoning**: can 12 sweets be shared fairly between 5 friends without cutting any? You can be *certain* the answer is no - try giving 2 each (10 used, 2 left over) or 3 each (15 needed, too many).
example_harder.answer: All four kinds - quantity, structure, pattern and reasoning - appear in one everyday problem.

word.text:
The name for this way of thinking is **mathematics** (often shortened to "maths" or "math").
It comes from the ancient Greek word *máthēma*, which meant "something that is learned".
To the ancient Greeks, mathematics was simply *the* subject you learn - the model of careful,
reliable knowledge.

l0-what-is-mathematics.no_symbol_note:
There is no symbol for "mathematics" itself. Mathematics *uses* symbols - and you will meet
your first ones in [[lesson:l0-symbols|Why do mathematical symbols exist?]] - but every symbol
is just a short name for an idea you will already understand.

formal.statement:
**Mathematics** is the study of quantity, structure, space, change and pattern, carried out by
logical reasoning from precisely stated definitions and assumptions.

(There is no single definition that every mathematician accepts; this is a widely used working
description.)

glossary.meaning: How many or how much.
How something is built or arranged - its parts and how they connect.
Shapes, sizes, positions and distances.
How one thing alters when another thing alters.
A regularity that lets you predict what comes next.
Reaching conclusions that *must* be true because of what you already know.
Exact statements of what words mean.
The starting facts an argument is allowed to use.

worked.title: The toy-car pattern
worked.problem: A child lines up toy cars in groups - 1 car, then 2 cars, then 3 cars. How many cars will the next group have, and which kinds of mathematical thinking did you use?
steps: Look at the groups: 1, 2, 3. Each group has one more car than the group before.
Noticing that "one more each time" is spotting a **pattern**.
Using the pattern to say the next group has 4 cars is a **prediction**.
Saying "4" at all is answering a question about **quantity**.
worked.answer: 4 cars. You used quantity and pattern - and a little reasoning to make the prediction.

experiment.task: Look at the staircase through all four lenses. Then add steps until it has 6, and see what each lens tells you.
experiment.success:
You have seen one object four ways. Notice that the *reasoning* lens tells you something about
a staircase you have not built yet. That ability - being sure about cases you never checked -
is what makes mathematics powerful.

mistakes.mistake: "Mathematics is just arithmetic (adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing)."
mistakes.why: Arithmetic is one tool inside mathematics, like a hammer inside a toolbox.
mistakes.fix: Think of mathematics as the study of quantity, pattern, structure and reasoning. Arithmetic is the part about calculating with quantities.

mistakes.mistake: "Being good at mathematics means being fast."
mistakes.why: Speed helps with routine calculation, but mathematical discoveries come from slow, careful thinking. Many great mathematicians describe themselves as slow thinkers.
mistakes.fix: Aim for understanding first. Speed, where it matters, comes later on its own.

mistakes.mistake: "Some people just have a maths brain, and I don't."
mistakes.why: Mathematics is learned like a language - one word, one idea at a time. Difficulty usually means an earlier rung of the ladder is missing, not that the learner cannot climb.
mistakes.fix: When something feels hard, look for the earlier idea it depends on. This course is built to help you find it.

statements.text: The word "mathematics" comes from the ancient Greek *máthēma*, meaning "that which is learned".
There is no single definition of mathematics that all mathematicians agree on.
statements.note: Philosophers of mathematics still debate what mathematics is *about*.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes mathematics?
questions.explanation: Mathematics studies quantity, pattern, structure and logical truth, and it uses exact reasoning to reach answers everyone can agree on.

options.text: The careful study of quantity, pattern, structure and what must be true, using exact reasoning.
Doing sums as quickly as possible.
options.diagnosis: Calculating is one part of mathematics, but mathematics is much more - patterns, shapes and reasoning too.
Formulas are summaries of ideas. Mathematics is about understanding the ideas and why they are true.

options.text: A collection of rules that were made up and have to be obeyed.
options.diagnosis: Mathematical facts are not arbitrary rules - they follow by reasoning from clear starting points.

questions.prompt: Which of these activities involve mathematical thinking? Choose all that apply.
questions.explanation: Arranging into equal rows (structure), house numbers (pattern) and being sure about the staircase (reasoning) are all mathematical. A favourite colour is a matter of taste.

options.text: Working out whether 20 chairs can be set out in equal rows of 6.
Noticing that the house numbers on one side of a street go up by 2 each time.
Being certain that a staircase with 10 steps (1 block, 2 blocks, ...) needs 10 blocks for its top step.

options.diagnosis: A favourite colour is a preference. There is no quantity, pattern or reasoning that decides it.

questions.prompt: True or false: mathematics is only about calculating the answers to sums.
questions.explanation: False. Calculation is one tool. Mathematics is the study of quantity, pattern, structure and what must be true.
questions.diagnosis: Calculating is part of mathematics, but mathematics also studies patterns, shapes, structures and logical truth.

questions.prompt: A staircase has steps of 1, 2, 3 and 4 blocks. How many blocks will step 5 have?
questions.hint: Each step has one more block than the step before.
questions.explanation: Each step has one more block than the one before, so step 5 has 5 blocks.

common_wrong.diagnosis: 10 is the total number of blocks in the first four steps. The question asks how many blocks are in step 5 alone.
15 is the total for the first five steps. The question asks about step 5 alone.

questions.prompt: In your own words, explain what mathematics is to a friend who thinks it is "just sums".
questions.explanation: A good explanation goes beyond sums to include patterns or structure, reasoning, and precision.
rubric: Mentions more than calculation - for example patterns, shapes or structure.
Mentions reasoning, or being sure that something must be true.
Mentions that mathematics is precise, or a language where statements mean exactly one thing.
questions.model_answer:
Mathematics is much more than sums. It is a precise way of thinking about how many and how
much, about patterns and what comes next, about shapes and how things are built, and about
what must be true. It is like a language where every sentence means exactly one thing, and
you can be certain of an answer because you have reasoned it out.

connections_forward.how: Next we look at why people invented mathematics in the first place.
Patterns get a lesson of their own.
The "what must be true" lens grows into the idea of proof.
The Riemann Hypothesis is a statement about a deep pattern in the prime numbers.
P versus NP is a question about the structure of problems and how hard they are to solve.

alternatives.title: A visitor from another planet
alternatives.text:
Imagine a visitor from another planet who speaks no human language. You cannot tell them
your name or the weather - but you can tap three times, then three times again, and they
can tap six. You can draw a triangle, a square and a pentagon, and they can draw a hexagon
next. You both now share something exact: quantities and patterns. Many scientists think
mathematics is the language we would use to talk with such a visitor, because it does not
depend on any particular culture. That is what mathematics is: the part of thinking that is
precise enough for anyone to share.

alternatives.title: What mathematics is NOT
alternatives.text:
Sometimes the clearest way to see something is to see what it is not.

- Mathematics is **not** a list of tricks for getting answers. The tricks come *after* the ideas.
- Mathematics is **not** about being fast. It is about being right, and knowing *why* you are right.
- Mathematics is **not** only about numbers. Shapes, patterns, networks and logic are mathematics too.
- Mathematics is **not** opinion. Two people who reason correctly always reach the same answer.

What is left when you remove those misunderstandings? A careful way of thinking about how
much, what comes next, how things are built and what must be true.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
Mathematics is the game of being *really* sure. How many cookies are in the jar? Let's count
and be sure. What comes after red, blue, red, blue, red? Blue! We can be sure because we see
the pattern. If I have more cookies than you, and you have more than your little brother,
do I have more than your brother? Yes - we can be sure without even counting his. Being
really sure about things like that is what mathematics is.

alternatives.title: Four questions
alternatives.text:
Try answering these, and notice the *kind* of thinking each needs.

1. How many legs do three cats have altogether? (*quantity*)
2. What comes next: 5, 10, 15, 20, ...? (*pattern*)
3. Can you build a square from 7 identical square tiles? (*structure*)
4. If every cat has four legs, and Tom is a cat, how many legs does Tom have? (*reasoning*)

Each answer is something everyone can agree on, once they think carefully. Mathematics is
the study of exactly these kinds of question.

l0-why-mathematics.goal:
We are learning why people invented mathematics, and the very first mathematical idea they
needed: matching things one-to-one.
l0-why-mathematics.why:
Mathematics was not handed down as a finished set of rules. People built it, step by step,
to solve real problems - keeping track of animals, trading, sharing, measuring land and
following the seasons. Seeing those problems makes the ideas feel natural rather than imposed.
l0-why-mathematics.problem: How can you be sure none of your sheep went missing - when you do not have words for numbers?
l0-why-mathematics.plain:
Long before there were written numbers, people needed to keep track of things: how many
animals left in the morning, how many baskets of grain were traded, how many days until the
river flooded.

The oldest trick is beautifully simple: **match things up**. For every sheep that leaves the
pen, put one pebble in a bag. In the evening, take out one pebble for every sheep that comes
back. If pebbles are left in the bag, some sheep are missing - and you know exactly how many
pebbles' worth.

You do not need number words to do this. You only need to pair each sheep with exactly one
pebble. Counting, written numbers and calculation all grew from this idea.

analogy.title: Coats and hooks
analogy.text:
At a party every guest hangs their coat on a hook. At the end of the night, if a coat is
still hanging, you know a guest has not left yet - even if you never counted the guests.
Each guest matched one hook. Matching like this tells you whether two groups are the same
size without saying a single number.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a pen of sheep and a bag of pebbles. In the morning, each sheep that
walks out adds one pebble to the bag. In the evening, each sheep that walks back in removes
one pebble. Any pebbles left at the end stand for sheep that have not come home.
visual.prompt: Send the sheep out, then bring them back. What do the leftover pebbles tell you?

example_simple.title: Cups and saucers
example_simple.problem: There are some cups and some saucers on a table. Without counting, how can you tell whether there are the same number of each?
steps: Put one cup on each saucer.
If every cup has a saucer and every saucer has a cup, the two groups are the same size.
If a cup is left without a saucer, there are more cups. If a saucer is left empty, there are more saucers.
example_simple.answer: Pair them up. Matching tells you which group is bigger, or that they are equal, without any counting.

example_harder.title: The returning flock
example_harder.problem: A shepherd put one pebble in a bag for each of her sheep in the morning. In the evening, she removes one pebble for each returning sheep, and 2 pebbles are left. What does she know?
steps: Every sheep that left was matched with one pebble.
Every sheep that returned removed exactly one pebble.
So each pebble still in the bag belongs to a sheep that did not return.
Two pebbles remain, so two sheep are still out - she knows this without ever saying "how many sheep" she owns.
example_harder.answer: Exactly two sheep are missing.

word.text:
Pairing two groups so that every member of each group has exactly one partner in the other
is called a **one-to-one correspondence**. "Correspondence" means "matching up". It is one of
the deepest ideas in mathematics: much later you will see it used to compare the sizes of
*infinite* collections.

symbols.name: tally marks
symbols.looks_like: Short upright strokes, one for each thing counted, often with every fifth stroke drawn across the other four.
symbols.means: One stroke stands for one object. A tally is a one-to-one correspondence written down.
symbols.why: Strokes are the easiest marks to make with a stick, a knife or a piece of chalk - which is why they are among the oldest number symbols in the world.
symbols.read_aloud: "Four tally marks", or simply the number they show - "four".

formal.statement:
A **one-to-one correspondence** between two collections is a way of pairing their members so
that every member of each collection is paired with exactly one member of the other.
Two collections have the same size exactly when such a pairing exists.

glossary.meaning: A group of things considered together, such as a flock of sheep or a bag of pebbles.
One of the things in a collection.
Linking things two at a time - one from each collection.
Not zero and not two or more - precisely one.

notation.read_aloud: six tally marks
notation.english: Six things have been matched with six strokes, so there are six things.

connections_back.how: Keeping track of animals is a problem about quantity - one of the four lenses of mathematics.

worked.title: Who is missing from the picnic?
worked.problem: Children leave a classroom for a picnic, and each one takes a sticker from a sheet as they go. When they come back, each child sticks their sticker back on the sheet. One space is still empty. What can the teacher conclude?
steps: Each child who left took exactly one sticker - a one-to-one correspondence between children and stickers.
Each child who came back returned exactly one sticker.
An empty space is a sticker that was not returned, so it belongs to a child who has not come back.
worked.answer: Exactly one child is still missing. The teacher knows this without counting the class.

experiment.task: Use the pebbles to discover how many sheep failed to return. Send all the sheep out, then bring back every sheep that comes home.
experiment.success:
The leftover pebbles told you how many sheep are missing - and you never needed to count the
flock. This is one-to-one correspondence: the idea underneath every act of counting.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking you must know number words to tell whether two groups are the same size.
mistakes.why: Matching works without any words at all. People (and even some animals) can compare groups by pairing.
mistakes.fix: Remember the cups and saucers. Pairing comes first; counting is a faster way of doing the same job.

mistakes.mistake: Matching one pebble with two sheep "to save pebbles".
mistakes.why: Then a missing sheep might not be noticed. The method only works if every sheep has exactly one pebble.
mistakes.fix: The rule is *exactly one partner each* - that is what "one-to-one" means.

statements.text: Bones with deliberately cut rows of notches, more than 20,000 years old, have been found in Africa.
Many archaeologists think such notches were tallies used to keep count of something.
statements.note: Nobody can be certain what was being counted - possibly days, animals or events.

statements.text: Small clay tokens used to keep records of goods appear in the ancient Near East from roughly 10,000 years ago, and written number signs developed there several thousand years later.

questions.prompt: Which of these were real reasons people developed mathematics? Choose all that apply.
questions.explanation: Mathematics grew from practical needs - tracking animals and goods, trade, measuring land and following the seasons.

options.text: Keeping track of animals and goods.
Following the seasons and making calendars.

options.diagnosis: Mathematics existed for thousands of years before schools. It grew from practical needs.

questions.prompt: A shepherd puts one pebble in a bag for each sheep that leaves. Later she removes one pebble for each sheep that returns, and 3 pebbles are left. How many sheep have not returned?
questions.hint: Each pebble belongs to exactly one sheep.
questions.explanation: Each leftover pebble matches one sheep that did not return, so 3 sheep are still out.

questions.prompt: True or false: to know whether two groups are the same size, you must know the number words.
questions.explanation: False. A one-to-one correspondence shows that two groups are the same size without counting.
questions.diagnosis: Pairing the members of the two groups one-to-one tells you whether they are the same size, with no words needed.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a one-to-one correspondence?
questions.explanation: One-to-one means every child has exactly one chair and every chair has exactly one child.

options.text: Every child in a class sits on their own chair, and no chair is empty.

options.diagnosis: Each chair has two partners, so the pairing is not one-to-one.

options.text: Every child sits on a chair, and three chairs are empty.
options.diagnosis: Three chairs have no partner, so not every member of the chairs group is matched.

questions.prompt: Explain in your own words why the shepherd's pebble method works, even though she has no words for numbers.
questions.explanation: The method works because of one-to-one matching - exactly one pebble per sheep.
rubric: Each sheep is matched with exactly one pebble.
A pebble left over means its sheep did not come back.
No counting or number words are needed - only matching.
questions.model_answer:
Every sheep that leaves gets exactly one pebble, and every sheep that returns takes exactly
one pebble away. So any pebble still in the bag belongs to a sheep that did not return. She
never needs number words - she only needs to match sheep and pebbles one-to-one.

connections_forward.how: Counting is one-to-one correspondence with the counting words.
Pairing objects is the most reliable way to compare two groups.
The formal name for a one-to-one correspondence is a bijection.
Cantor used correspondences to show some infinite collections are bigger than others - an idea at the heart of computability.

alternatives.title: Try it with your hands
alternatives.text:
Put some coins on the table in one pile and some buttons in another - grab a random handful
of each, without counting. Now place one button on top of each coin. Do not count anything.
When you run out of one kind, look at what is left: if coins are left uncovered, there were
more coins; if buttons are left over, there were more buttons; if neither, they were the
same. You have just compared two quantities using one-to-one correspondence - exactly what
the first mathematicians did.

alternatives.title: How tallies became numbers
alternatives.text:
Archaeologists have found bones tens of thousands of years old with neat rows of cut
notches. Many think these were tallies - one notch per thing. Much later, in the ancient
Near East, people used small clay tokens to stand for goods: one token per jar of oil.
Eventually they pressed the tokens' shapes into clay instead of keeping the tokens, and
those marks became some of the first written number signs. Each step made the record
shorter, but underneath was always the same idea: one mark for one thing.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
Imagine you have some toy cars and some toy garages. You want to know if every car can have
its own garage. Don't count! Just drive one car into each garage. If a car has no garage
left, there are more cars. If a garage is empty, there are more garages. If everything
fits perfectly, they are the same. Grown-up mathematicians call this "one-to-one
correspondence".

l1-bigger-smaller.goal:
We are learning the symbols $>$ ("greater than") and $<$ ("less than"), how to read them, and how to
write them the right way round.
l1-bigger-smaller.why:
Comparisons are among the most common statements in mathematics. Statements built from $<$ and
$>$ describe where zeta zeros may lie and how fast running times grow - they are everywhere in
research mathematics.
l1-bigger-smaller.problem:
How do we write "seven is more than three" in a short, exact, universal way - and never get it
backwards?
l1-bigger-smaller.plain:
Two symbols compare numbers:

- $7 > 3$ is read "seven is **greater than** three".
- $3 < 7$ is read "three is **less than** seven".

The trick to remember: the symbol is **wide open on the side of the bigger number** and **pointed
on the side of the smaller number**. Many people picture a hungry mouth that always opens toward
the bigger meal.

Notice that $7 > 3$ and $3 < 7$ say exactly the same fact - one reads it from the big number, the
other from the small number.

If two numbers are the same, neither symbol is true: $5 > 5$ is false and $5 < 5$ is false.
(For equal numbers we use $=$, from the next lesson.)

analogy.title: The open mouth
analogy.text:
Picture a crocodile choosing between 3 fish and 7 fish. It opens its mouth toward the 7 - it
always wants the bigger pile. Draw the mouth and you have $3 < 7$ or $7 > 3$. The open side faces
the bigger number, the point faces the smaller one.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: two groups with their numbers, and the comparison symbol between them. As
you change the groups, the symbol turns to keep its open side toward the bigger group. When the
groups are equal it becomes $=$.
visual.prompt: Change the groups and say the statement aloud each time - "... is greater than ..." or "... is less than ...".

example_simple.title: Seven and three
example_simple.problem: Write a true statement comparing 7 and 3 using $>$ or $<$.
steps: 7 is the bigger number, so the open side faces 7.
Writing 7 first - $7 > 3$, "seven is greater than three".
Writing 3 first - $3 < 7$, "three is less than seven".

example_harder.title: Forty-five and fifty-four
example_harder.problem: Put the right symbol between 45 and 54.
steps: Compare tens first - 4 tens versus 5 tens. 54 is bigger.
The open side must face 54, and 45 is written first.
So the point faces 45 - $45 < 54$.
example_harder.answer: $45 < 54$, "forty-five is less than fifty-four".

word.text:
$>$ is called the **greater-than sign** and $<$ the **less-than sign**. Statements built with them
are called **inequalities** - a word you will meet again in algebra.

symbols.name: greater-than sign
symbols.looks_like: Two short lines meeting at a point on the right, open on the left.
symbols.means: The number on the left (open side) is bigger than the number on the right.
symbols.why: The shape shows size - wide on the big side, narrow on the small side. It was introduced by the English mathematician Thomas Harriot, published in 1631.
symbols.read_aloud: "Is greater than" - $9 > 2$ is "nine is greater than two".

symbols.name: less-than sign
symbols.looks_like: Two short lines meeting at a point on the left, open on the right.
symbols.means: The number on the left (pointed side) is smaller than the number on the right.
symbols.why: The same shape turned around. Pointed side - smaller.
symbols.read_aloud: "Is less than" - $2 < 9$ is "two is less than nine".

formal.statement:
For numbers $a$ and $b$, $a < b$ ("$a$ is less than $b$") means $a$ comes before $b$ in the order of
numbers, and $a > b$ ("$a$ is greater than $b$") means $a$ comes after $b$. The statements $a < b$
and $b > a$ say the same thing.

glossary.meaning: Any two numbers.
The order in which they come when counting up.
One is true exactly when the other is true.

notation.read_aloud: three is less than seven

parts.meaning: Is less than - the point faces the smaller number.

notation.english: Three is smaller than seven.

notation.read_aloud: seven is greater than three

parts.meaning: Is greater than - the open side faces the bigger number.

notation.english: The same fact, read from the other end.

connections_back.how: These symbols write down the result of comparing two numbers.

worked.title: Over one hundred
worked.problem: Which symbol goes between 102 and 99?
steps: 102 has a hundreds digit; 99 does not. So 102 is bigger.
The open side faces 102, which is written first.

experiment.task: Change the groups so that the statement shown reads "left is greater than right".
experiment.success:
The symbol now opens toward the left group. Read it aloud: "... is greater than ...". The symbol
is just a picture of which side is bigger.

mistakes.mistake: Writing the symbol backwards ($3 > 7$).
mistakes.why: The open side must face the bigger number.
mistakes.fix: Draw the open "mouth" toward the bigger number first, then check by reading aloud.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking $3 < 7$ and $7 > 3$ are different facts.
mistakes.why: They describe the same comparison from opposite ends.
mistakes.fix: Read both aloud - "three is less than seven", "seven is greater than three" - same fact.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking $5 < 5$ is true.
mistakes.why: 5 is not smaller than itself.
mistakes.fix: For equal numbers, use $=$.

statements.text: The symbols $<$ and $>$ first appeared in a book by Thomas Harriot published in 1631, ten years after his death.

questions.prompt: How is $12 > 8$ read aloud?
questions.explanation: $>$ means "is greater than" - twelve is greater than eight.

options.diagnosis: The open side faces 12, so 12 is the bigger number - "greater than".
Read from left to right - twelve comes first.

questions.prompt: Which statement says the same thing as $4 < 9$?
questions.explanation: "Four is less than nine" is the same fact as "nine is greater than four".

options.diagnosis: This says nine is less than four, which is false.
This says four is greater than nine, which is false.

questions.prompt: True or false: $5 < 5$.
questions.explanation: False. $5 = 5$, so neither $<$ nor $>$ is true.
questions.diagnosis: 5 is not smaller than itself - the numbers are equal.

questions.prompt: Explain how you remember which way round to write $<$ and $>$.
questions.explanation: Open side to the bigger number, point to the smaller.
rubric: The open (wide) side faces the bigger number.
The pointed side faces the smaller number.
questions.model_answer: The symbol opens wide toward the bigger number, like a mouth reaching for the bigger meal, and its point faces the smaller number.

connections_forward.how: The third possibility - equal - and the equals sign.
Reading inequalities fluently, including with negative numbers.
The critical strip of the zeta function is described by two inequalities.

alternatives.title: Big side, small side
alternatives.text:
Draw $<$ large on paper. Measure the two ends: the right end is wide open, the left end is a
single point. Now write a big number at the wide end and a small number at the point - 2 < 9.
The symbol itself is a little picture: it is *bigger* where the bigger number is.

alternatives.title: Three steps every time
alternatives.text:
1. Decide which number is bigger (count, or compare tens first).
2. Draw the open side facing the bigger number.
3. Read it aloud from left to right. If it sounds right ("nine is greater than two"), it is right.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
This sign < is a hungry crocodile mouth. The crocodile always eats the bigger number! So the
open mouth points at the bigger one: 2 < 9, because 9 is bigger and the crocodile wants it.

l1-comparing-numbers.goal:
We are learning to compare two numbers - deciding which is larger - by matching, by counting
order, and by looking at tens and ones.
l1-comparing-numbers.why:
Comparing numbers lets us rank, sort and decide. Later, the order of numbers becomes the number
line, inequalities, and statements like "this algorithm takes fewer steps than that one".
l1-comparing-numbers.problem: Given two numbers, how can you tell which is larger - even when you cannot see the objects?
l1-comparing-numbers.plain:
There are three good ways to compare two numbers.

1. **Match objects.** Make a group for each number and pair them up. The group with objects left
   over has the larger number.
2. **Use counting order.** When counting up from 1, the larger number is the one you reach
   *later*. 9 comes after 6, so 9 is larger.
3. **Look at tens first.** For two-digit numbers, compare the tens digits first: 34 has 3 tens and
   29 has only 2 tens, so 34 is larger - whatever the ones digits are. Only if the tens are equal do
   you compare the ones.

When one number is larger, we can also ask **how many more** it is: 9 is 3 more than 6.

analogy.title: Queueing up
analogy.text:
People in a queue are given tickets in order: 1, 2, 3, ... Someone holding ticket 9 arrived later
than someone holding ticket 6 - and more people had arrived by then. A later ticket number is a
bigger number.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: two groups with their numbers shown underneath. Lines pair the objects
one-to-one. Objects without a partner are highlighted - they show how many more the larger group
has.
visual.prompt: Change the two groups. How many objects are left unpaired each time?

example_simple.title: Six or nine?
example_simple.problem: Which is larger, 6 or 9? How many more?
steps: Counting up - one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. 9 comes after 6.
So 9 is larger.
From 6, count on to 9 - seven, eight, nine. That is three more counts.

example_harder.title: Tens first
example_harder.problem: Which is larger, 29 or 34?
steps: Look at the tens digits - 29 has 2 tens and 34 has 3 tens.
Three tens (thirty) is more than two tens (twenty).
Even the biggest number with 2 tens, 29, is less than 30, and 34 is beyond 30.
The ones digits (9 and 4) do not matter here.
example_harder.answer: 34 is larger. Comparing tens first avoids being fooled by the 9.

word.text:
This is **comparison** of numbers. The larger number is also called the **greater** number, and
the smaller one the **lesser** number. "How many more" is the **difference** between them - you
will learn to calculate differences in Level 2.

l1-comparing-numbers.no_symbol_note:
The symbols for "greater than" and "less than" are introduced in the very next lesson,
[[lesson:l1-bigger-smaller|Bigger and smaller]].

formal.statement:
For counting numbers $a$ and $b$, $a$ is **less than** $b$ when $a$ comes before $b$ in the counting
sequence; equivalently, when a collection of $a$ objects can be matched one-to-one with part of a
collection of $b$ objects, leaving some of the $b$ objects unmatched.

glossary.meaning: Letters standing for any two counting numbers.
one, two, three, ... in order.
Some, but not all, of its objects.
Without a partner.

connections_back.how: Tens and ones come from counting in groups of ten.
Comparison of quantities, now applied to numbers.

worked.title: Stickers
worked.problem: Ana has 34 stickers and Ben has 43. Who has more?
steps: Compare tens first - Ana has 3 tens, Ben has 4 tens.
Four tens is more than three tens.
worked.answer: Ben has more. The digits are the same, but their places differ.

experiment.task: Change the groups so that the left group is smaller than the right group.
experiment.success:
The left group now runs out first when pairing - every left object has a partner, but some right
objects do not. That is exactly what "smaller" means.

mistakes.mistake: Comparing the ones digits first (thinking 29 > 34 because 9 > 4).
mistakes.why: The tens digit is worth ten times as much, so it decides first.
mistakes.fix: Always compare the biggest place first - tens before ones, hundreds before tens.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking a number made of bigger digits is always larger (thinking 98 > 102).
mistakes.why: 102 has a hundreds digit; 98 has none.
mistakes.fix: Count the digits first - a three-digit counting number is always larger than a two-digit one.

questions.prompt: Which is larger, 52 or 48?
questions.explanation: 5 tens is more than 4 tens, so 52 is larger.

options.diagnosis: 48 has the bigger ones digit, but 52 has more tens - five tens beats four tens.

questions.prompt: How many more is 11 than 8? (Count on from 8.)
questions.hint: Count on from 8 - nine, ten, eleven.
questions.explanation: Counting on from 8 - nine, ten, eleven - takes three counts.

questions.prompt: True or false: 98 is larger than 102, because 9 and 8 are bigger digits than 1, 0 and 2.
questions.explanation: False. 102 is larger - it has a hundred.
questions.diagnosis: 102 has one hundred, while 98 has no hundreds. The hundreds place decides first.

questions.prompt: Explain how to decide which of 67 and 76 is larger.
questions.explanation: Compare tens first - 7 tens beats 6 tens.
rubric: Compare the tens digits first.
76 has 7 tens and 67 has 6 tens, so 76 is larger.
questions.model_answer: Look at the tens first. 76 has seven tens and 67 has only six tens, so 76 is larger - the ones digits do not matter here.

connections_forward.how: Symbols for comparing - greater than and less than.
The order of numbers as positions on a line.
"How many more" becomes subtraction.

alternatives.title: Towers of blocks
alternatives.text:
Build a tower of 6 blocks and a tower of 9 blocks side by side. The taller tower is the larger
number, and the blocks sticking up above the shorter tower show how many more - 3. For bigger
numbers, build towers of tens: 34 is three tall ten-towers and four single blocks; 29 is two
ten-towers and nine single blocks. Put them next to each other and 34 clearly wins.

alternatives.title: Digits versus places
alternatives.text:
Look at 34 and 43. They use exactly the same digits. But in 34, the 3 is in the tens place and
means thirty; in 43, the 4 is in the tens place and means forty. Comparing numbers is about the
*values of the places*, not just which digits appear.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
You have 6 sweets and your friend has 9. Line them up, one of yours next to one of theirs. Your
line stops first! Your friend still has 3 left with no partner. So 9 is more than 6 - by 3.

l1-composite-numbers.goal:
We are learning what composite numbers are - whole numbers bigger than 1 that are not prime - and that
every whole number bigger than 1 is either prime or composite.
l1-composite-numbers.why:
Splitting the numbers above 1 into primes and composites is the first step toward breaking every number
into its prime building blocks - a central tool in number theory.
l1-composite-numbers.problem: If prime numbers refuse to form rectangles, what do we call the numbers that can?
l1-composite-numbers.plain:
A whole number bigger than 1 that **can** be arranged into a real rectangle - at least 2 rows, at least 2
in each row - is called **composite**.

- 4 is 2 rows of 2 - composite.
- 6 is 2 rows of 3 - composite.
- 9 is 3 rows of 3 - composite.
- 12 is 3 rows of 4 (or 2 rows of 6) - composite.

**Every whole number bigger than 1 is exactly one of the two**: prime (no rectangle) or composite (at
least one rectangle). It cannot be both and cannot be neither.

And **1 is special**: it is neither prime nor composite.

A composite number is "composed" of smaller pieces: each side of its rectangle is a smaller number, and
those can be broken down further until only primes are left - $12 = 3 \times 4 = 3 \times 2 \times 2$.

analogy.title: A brick wall
analogy.text:
A composite number is like a wall built from rows of bricks - you can see the rows. A prime number is like
a single unbreakable plank: there is no way to stack it into rows.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: 12 tiles arranged in equal rows. Each successful rectangle (with at least two rows of
at least two tiles) is proof that 12 is composite.
visual.prompt: Find every rectangle 12 tiles can make. Then try 13.

example_simple.title: Six
example_simple.problem: Is 6 prime or composite?
steps: Try 2 rows - 3 tiles each, nothing left over.
A real rectangle exists.

example_harder.title: Prime, composite or neither?
example_harder.problem: Classify 1, 2 and 25.
steps: 1 is neither - primes and composites are both defined to be bigger than 1.
2 can only make one row of 2 - prime.
25 makes 5 rows of 5 - composite, even though it is odd.
example_harder.answer: 1 is neither, 2 is prime, 25 is composite.

word.text:
These are **composite numbers** - from Latin *compositus*, "put together" - because they are put together
from smaller factors.

l1-composite-numbers.no_symbol_note:
There is no special symbol for "composite". What we write instead is the rectangle itself, as a
multiplication - $12 = 3 \times 4$ shows at once that 12 is composite.

formal.statement:
A natural number $n$ is **composite** if $n > 1$ and $n$ is not prime; equivalently, if $n = a \times b$
for some natural numbers $a$ and $b$ with $1 < a < n$ and $1 < b < n$.

glossary.meaning: $n$ is bigger than 1.
$n$ tiles make $a$ rows of $b$.
$a$ is bigger than 1 and smaller than $n$ - a real rectangle, not a single row.

notation.read_aloud: twelve equals three times four equals three times two times two

parts.meaning: A rectangle of 3 rows of 4 - proof 12 is composite.
Breaking the 4 further, until only primes remain.

notation.english: Twelve is built from the primes 3, 2 and 2.

connections_back.how: Composite numbers are exactly the numbers above 1 that are not prime.

worked.title: Four in a row
worked.problem: Classify 21, 23, 25 and 27.
steps: 21 - 3 rows of 7 - composite.
23 - no rectangle works (try 2, 3, 4 and 5 rows - all leave tiles over) - prime.
25 - 5 rows of 5 - composite.
27 - 3 rows of 9 - composite.
worked.answer: 21, 25 and 27 are composite; 23 is prime.

experiment.task: Show that 21 is composite by finding a rectangle with more than one row.
experiment.success:
21 is 3 rows of 7. One rectangle is all it takes to prove a number is composite - it is a certificate you
can check at a glance.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking 1 is composite (or prime).
mistakes.why: Both words are defined only for numbers bigger than 1.
mistakes.fix: 1 is in a category of its own.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking only even numbers are composite.
mistakes.why: 9, 15, 21, 25 and 27 are odd and composite.
mistakes.fix: Test for rows of 3, 5 and 7, not just 2.

statements.text: Every natural number greater than 1 is either prime or composite, but not both.
Every composite number can be written as a product of prime numbers.
statements.note: In fact in exactly one way (apart from order) - the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, proved in Level 10.

questions.prompt: Which of these are composite? Choose all that apply.
questions.explanation: 9 (3 rows of 3) and 20 (4 rows of 5) are composite.

options.diagnosis: 17 makes no rectangle except a single row, so it is prime.
1 is neither prime nor composite.

questions.prompt: Which number is neither prime nor composite?
questions.explanation: 1 is neither prime nor composite.

options.diagnosis: 2 is prime.
Good thought - the words prime and composite are only used for natural numbers above 1, so 0 is not described by them either. But among counting numbers the special one is 1.

questions.prompt: True or false: every composite number is even.
questions.explanation: False. 9, 15 and 21 are odd composite numbers.
questions.diagnosis: 9 = 3 rows of 3 is odd and composite - a counterexample.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a prime number and a composite number, with an example of each.
questions.explanation: Composite numbers make rectangles; primes do not.
rubric: A composite number (bigger than 1) can be arranged into a rectangle with at least two rows of at least two; a prime cannot.
Gives a correct example of each (for example 7 prime, 8 composite).
questions.model_answer:
Both are whole numbers bigger than 1. A composite number can be arranged into a real rectangle, like 8
which is 2 rows of 4. A prime cannot - like 7, which only makes a single row.

connections_forward.how: The sides of the rectangles are the factors.
Breaking composite numbers all the way down to primes.
Why that breakdown is unique.

alternatives.title: Two kinds of number (and one oddball)
alternatives.text:
Sort the numbers 1 to 12:

- **Neither:** 1
- **Prime** (only a single row): 2, 3, 5, 7, 11
- **Composite** (at least one rectangle): 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12

Every number from 2 onward lands in exactly one of the last two groups.

alternatives.title: Packaging
alternatives.text:
A factory packs biscuits in rectangular trays. 24 biscuits can be packed as 4 by 6, 3 by 8 or 2 by 12 -
24 is composite. 23 biscuits cannot be packed into any tray with at least two rows, unless every row has
only one biscuit - 23 is prime, and the factory would hate it.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
Some numbers of blocks can make a rectangle with rows, like 6 blocks in 2 rows of 3. Those numbers are
called composite. Numbers that can only make a line are prime. And 1 block? It's too small to be either!

l1-counting-meaning.goal:
We are learning the exact rules that make counting work, and the word for the result of
counting: cardinality.
l1-counting-meaning.why:
You can already count. Now we make the method precise - every rule stated, nothing left to
habit. This is how mathematics treats every idea: make the familiar exact. The same habit, later,
lets us count the steps of algorithms and even compare the sizes of infinite collections.
l1-counting-meaning.problem: Exactly what rules must you follow so that counting always gives the right answer?
l1-counting-meaning.plain:
Counting works because of five simple rules:

1. **One word per object.** Every object gets exactly one counting word, and no word is used twice.
2. **Same order every time.** The words always come in the order one, two, three, four, ...
3. **The last word is the answer.** The last word said tells you how many there are.
4. **Anything can be counted.** Apples, sounds, ideas, or a mixture of different things.
5. **Order of objects does not matter.** Count left to right, right to left or in any jumble - same answer.

The answer counting gives - "how many objects are in this collection" - has a special name:
the **cardinality** of the collection.

analogy.title: Numbered seats
analogy.text:
Picture an empty cinema whose seats are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... in order. People walk in and fill
the seats from seat 1 upward, one person per seat. When everyone is seated, the number on the
last filled seat is how many people came. Counting is filling numbered seats: one object per
seat, seats in order, last seat number is the total.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a tray of balls. Tapping a ball gives it the next counting number, so the
tags always go 1, 2, 3, ... in order. A ball that already has a number cannot be tapped again.
The total shown is the last number given out. Shuffle and recount to test rule 5.
visual.prompt: Count the balls in two different orders. Do you ever get a different total?

example_simple.title: Two orders, one answer
example_simple.problem: Six coins are counted left to right, then right to left. What happens?
steps: Left to right - one, two, three, four, five, six.
Right to left - one, two, three, four, five, six. Different coins get each word this time.
In both counts each coin got exactly one word, in the standard order.
example_simple.answer: Both counts end on six. The cardinality is 6 whichever order we use.

example_harder.title: Counting a mixture
example_harder.problem: A bowl contains 2 apples and 3 oranges. Can you count them together, and what does the answer mean?
steps: Rule 4 says anything can be counted - so yes.
One (apple), two (apple), three (orange), four (orange), five (orange).
The answer counts *pieces of fruit*, not apples or oranges separately.
example_harder.answer: There are 5 pieces of fruit. You can count any collection - you just have to be clear what you are counting.

word.text:
The number of objects in a collection - the result of counting it - is called the
**cardinality** of the collection, from the Latin *cardo*, "hinge" or "pivot", because it is
the pivotal fact about how big the collection is. Numbers used this way ("how many") are
