sometimes called **cardinal numbers**.

l1-counting-meaning.no_symbol_note:
In later levels, mathematicians write the cardinality of a collection $A$ as $|A|$ - see
[[lesson:l8-sets|Sets]]. For now, "the number of things in the collection" is all we need.

formal.statement:
The **cardinality** of a finite collection is the counting number reached by matching its
objects one-to-one with the counting words "one, two, three, ..." in their standard order; it is
the last word used. Two finite collections have the same cardinality exactly when they can be
put in one-to-one correspondence.

glossary.meaning: Ending - a collection whose counting stops.
One word per object and one object per word.
one, two, three, ... - the same every time.
A matching between two collections.

connections_back.how: Counting finds which number a collection has.
Here the method of counting is made precise.

worked.title: A broken count
worked.problem: A child counts four toys by saying "one, two, three, five". Which rule did they break, and how many toys are there?
steps: Each toy got exactly one word, so rule 1 was followed.
But the words were not in the standard order - "four" was skipped. Rule 2 was broken.
Because the order was broken, the last word ("five") is not the cardinality.
Recount correctly - one, two, three, four.
worked.answer: Rule 2 (same order every time) was broken. There are 4 toys.

experiment.task: Build a tray with exactly 8 fish, then count them by tapping to check.
experiment.success:
Your tray has cardinality 8. Whatever order you tapped them in, the last number was 8 - that is
rule 5 at work.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping or repeating a counting word ("one, two, four").
mistakes.why: The last word then no longer matches the number of objects.
mistakes.fix: Say the counting words in their exact order.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking you cannot count a mixture of different things.
mistakes.why: Counting works for any collection - but the answer counts the whole mixture.
mistakes.fix: Say what you are counting ("pieces of fruit") and count away.

statements.text: The psychologists Rochel Gelman and Randy Gallistel (1978) identified five principles of counting - one-to-one, stable order, cardinal (last word is the total), abstraction (anything can be counted) and order-irrelevance.
Counting a finite collection in any order gives the same cardinality.

questions.prompt: Ravi counts five cups - "one, two, three, four, five" - but points at the first cup twice. Which counting rule did he break?
questions.explanation: One cup got two words, so the count is too big - there are really 4 cups.

options.diagnosis: His words were in the right order - the problem is that one cup received two words.
Cups can certainly be counted - that is not where things went wrong.

questions.prompt: True or false: you can count a collection made of 3 pencils and 2 rubbers together, getting 5 objects.
questions.explanation: True - the collection has cardinality 5.
questions.diagnosis: Anything can be counted together - the answer is the number of objects in the whole collection.

questions.prompt: When counting the books on a shelf, the last word said is "nineteen". What is the cardinality of the collection of books?
questions.explanation: The last counting word is the cardinality.

questions.prompt: In your own words, list the rules that make counting give the right answer.
questions.explanation: One word per object, standard order, last word is the total, order of objects irrelevant.
rubric: Each object gets exactly one counting word.
The counting words are said in their standard order.
The last word is the number of objects (the cardinality).
The order of the objects does not matter (or anything can be counted).
questions.model_answer:
Give each object exactly one counting word, say the words in the usual order (one, two,
three...), and the last word you say is how many there are. It does not matter which order
you go through the objects in, and you can count any kind of things.

connections_forward.how: What is the cardinality of an empty collection?
Cardinality of sets, written $|A|$.
Cantor showed some infinite collections have bigger cardinality than others - an idea used to prove limits of computation.

alternatives.title: The robot that could not count
alternatives.text:
An engineer built a robot to count boxes in a warehouse. On day one it counted some boxes
twice. The engineer added a rule: "mark each box after counting it". On day two it said "one,
three, two..." because it chose words at random. Rule two: "say the words in order". On day
three it said the last word but reported "box 47 is the last one" instead of "there are 47
boxes". Rule three: "the last word is the total". With three rules in place, the robot counted
perfectly. Children learn these same rules - usually without anyone saying them out loud.

alternatives.title: Check each rule, one at a time
alternatives.text:
After any count, ask three quick questions:

1. Did every object get a word, and only one? (If unsure, count again, moving each object as you go.)
2. Did I say the words in the right order, without skipping? (Say them slowly.)
3. Am I using the last word as the answer? (Not the first, not a favourite.)

Three "yes" answers mean the count is right.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
When you count your toys, touch each toy once - only once! - and say the numbers in order:
one, two, three. Don't skip any numbers. When you touch the last toy, the number you say is how
many toys you have. That's all counting is.

l1-counting-objects.goal: We are learning how to count large collections reliably by grouping objects into tens.
l1-counting-objects.why:
Counting one by one works for 5 objects but becomes slow and error-prone for 50 or 500.
Grouping into tens is the practical trick - and it is exactly the idea behind the way we write
numbers, which comes next.
l1-counting-objects.problem: How can you count a big, messy collection without losing your place?
l1-counting-objects.plain:
For a large collection, counting one by one is risky - lose concentration once and you must
start again. A better method:

1. **Make groups of ten.** Count out ten objects and push them together into a bundle.
2. **Keep making bundles** until fewer than ten objects are left.
3. **Count the bundles in tens** - ten, twenty, thirty, ...
4. **Then count on the loose objects** one at a time.

Because each bundle is checked separately, a mistake only costs you one bundle, not the whole
count. And the answer comes out in a very useful form: "4 tens and 7 ones" is 47.

Grouping never changes the total: it is just counting in a well-organised order, and the order
of counting never changes the answer.

analogy.title: Counting money
analogy.text:
A shop assistant counting a pile of coins stacks them in piles of ten. Five stacks and three
loose coins? That is fifty-three coins - counted in a few seconds, and easy to double-check by
glancing at the stacks.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a large group of stars. The "Bundle tens" button gathers loose stars into
groups of ten, drawn as boxes. The display shows how many tens and how many loose ones there are,
and the total.
visual.prompt: Bundle the stars into tens. How many tens and how many ones? What is the total?

example_simple.title: Straws
example_simple.problem: There are some straws on a table. You make 2 bundles of ten, and 3 straws are left over. How many straws are there?
steps: Count the bundles in tens - ten, twenty.
Count on the 3 loose straws - twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three.

example_harder.title: A messy pile
example_harder.problem: About fifty buttons are scattered in a heap. Describe how to count them accurately.
steps: Pick up buttons one at a time, counting to ten, and put each ten in its own small pile.
Suppose you make 4 piles of ten, and 7 buttons are left that cannot make another ten.
Count the piles in tens - ten, twenty, thirty, forty.
Count on the loose buttons - forty-one, forty-two, ..., forty-seven.
example_harder.answer: 47 buttons - 4 tens and 7 ones.

word.text:
A group of ten is simply called **a ten**, and a single loose object **a one**. Grouping in tens
is called **base ten** counting, because ten is the "base" size of each group. Humans probably
chose ten because we have ten fingers.

l1-counting-objects.no_symbol_note:
Grouping into tens is the idea behind our numerals: in 47, the 4 counts tens and the 7 counts
ones. That is the subject of the next lesson on [[lesson:l1-number-symbols|number symbols]].

formal.statement:
If a finite collection is split into groups of ten with some objects left over (fewer than ten),
then its cardinality equals ten for each group, counted on by the number of objects left over.
Grouping does not change the cardinality.

glossary.meaning: A collection whose counting ends.
The number of objects in the collection.
Continuing to count from a number, rather than from one.

notation.read_aloud: four tens and seven ones equals forty-seven
notation.english: Four bundles of ten and seven single objects make forty-seven.

connections_back.how: Counting on, one more each time.
Grouping is counting in a particular order, so the cardinality is unchanged.

worked.title: Counting a jar of marbles
worked.problem: You bundle marbles in tens and get 6 full bundles and 0 loose marbles. How many marbles?
steps: Six tens - ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty.
No loose marbles to count on.
worked.answer: 60 marbles. The 0 says there are no loose ones.

experiment.task: Build a collection of exactly 26 apples, using bundles to check your count.
experiment.success:
26 is 2 tens and 6 ones. Bundling let you check the count at a glance - and notice the 2 and the
6 in the numeral 26 tell you exactly how many tens and ones there are.

mistakes.mistake: Counting bundles as ones ("4 bundles and 7 loose make 11").
mistakes.why: Each bundle stands for ten objects, not one.
mistakes.fix: Count bundles in tens - ten, twenty, thirty, forty - and then count on the ones.

mistakes.mistake: Making bundles of different sizes.
mistakes.why: The method only works if every bundle has exactly ten.
mistakes.fix: Check each bundle before setting it aside.

statements.text: Humans probably count in tens because we have ten fingers.
statements.note: Some cultures have counted in twenties (fingers and toes) or twelves; the Babylonians used sixty.

questions.prompt: You make 5 bundles of ten pencils, and 3 pencils are left over. How many pencils are there?
questions.explanation: 5 tens is fifty, and 3 more is 53.

common_wrong.diagnosis: Each bundle holds ten pencils, so 5 bundles are fifty, not five.
The 5 bundles are tens (fifty) and the 3 loose pencils are ones - fifty-three.

questions.prompt: Why is grouping into tens helpful when counting a large collection?
questions.explanation: Grouping organises the count without changing the total.

options.text: Mistakes are easier to avoid and check, and the result matches how we write numbers.
It changes the total to a rounder number.
options.diagnosis: Grouping never changes the total - it only organises the count.

options.text: Tens are the only numbers that can be counted.
options.diagnosis: Any number can be counted. Tens are just a convenient group size.

questions.prompt: A pile is bundled into 7 tens and 0 loose ones. How many objects is that?
questions.explanation: 7 tens and no ones is 70.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would count about a hundred paper clips quickly and accurately.
questions.explanation: Bundle into tens, count the tens, count on the ones.
rubric: Make groups (bundles) of ten.
Count the groups in tens.
Count on the loose ones that do not make a full ten.
questions.model_answer:
I would count out groups of ten paper clips and put each group in its own pile. Then I would
count the piles in tens - ten, twenty, thirty and so on - and count on any loose clips one
at a time.

connections_forward.how: Our way of writing numbers records tens and ones by position.
Counting in equal groups of other sizes.
Grouping in tens is the secret behind written addition.

alternatives.title: Do it with pasta
alternatives.text:
Pour out a handful of dried pasta (or rice grains, or coins). Count out ten and put them in a
cup. Then ten more in another cup. When you cannot make another ten, stop. Count the cups by
saying "ten, twenty, thirty..." and then count the loose pieces. You will find this is much
faster - and if you lose your place, you only need to recount one cup.

alternatives.title: Eggs in boxes
alternatives.text:
Eggs are sold in boxes of six or twelve, so that shopkeepers can count them quickly - nobody
counts eggs one by one in a shop. Bundling into tens is the same idea, with ten as the box
size. Box sizes make large counts quick and reliable.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
If you have lots and lots of blocks, it is hard to count them all. So let's make towers of 10
blocks! Count the towers: ten, twenty, thirty. Then count the blocks that are left over:
thirty-one, thirty-two. That's a much easier way to count lots of things.

l1-decimals.goal:
We are learning how decimals extend place value to the right of a point - tenths, hundredths,
thousandths - and how they connect to fractions.
l1-decimals.why:
Decimals are how measurements, money and computer calculations are usually written. Understanding
them as place value (not as "numbers with a dot") avoids the most common decimal mistakes - and later
helps explain why computers store numbers only approximately.
l1-decimals.problem: How can we write parts of a whole using the same place-value idea that writes whole numbers?
l1-decimals.plain:
Place value works to the left: ones, tens, hundreds - each place ten times bigger. Run it the other way
and each place to the **right** is ten times **smaller**:

- after the ones come the **tenths** ($\tfrac{1}{10}$),
- then the **hundredths** ($\tfrac{1}{100}$),
- then the **thousandths** ($\tfrac{1}{1000}$).

A **decimal point** marks where the ones end and the parts begin. So **3.25** means 3 ones, 2 tenths
and 5 hundredths - three and a quarter.

Some useful facts:

- $0.5 = \tfrac{5}{10} = \tfrac{1}{2}$ (one half),
- $0.25 = \tfrac{25}{100} = \tfrac{1}{4}$ (one quarter),
- $0.75 = \tfrac{3}{4}$.

**Comparing decimals:** compare place by place from the left, exactly as with whole numbers. $0.5$ is
bigger than $0.45$ - it has 5 tenths, while $0.45$ has only 4 tenths - even though "45" looks bigger
than "5".

analogy.title: Money
analogy.text:
In many currencies, 2.75 means 2 whole units and 75 hundredths of a unit (75 cents or pence). The point
separates whole units from the parts. A price of 0.50 is half a unit - 50 hundredths - which is the same
as 0.5, five tenths.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: one whole drawn as a square of 100 small squares (10 rows of 10). Each small
square is one hundredth; each full row is one tenth. The shaded amount is shown as a fraction of 100
and as a decimal.
visual.prompt: Shade exactly one row. Then shade 5 rows. What decimals do you get?

example_simple.title: Seven tenths
example_simple.problem: Write $\tfrac{7}{10}$ as a decimal.
steps: $\tfrac{7}{10}$ is 7 tenths.
Tenths go in the first place after the decimal point.
There are no ones, so write 0 before the point.

example_harder.title: The longer-looks-bigger trap
example_harder.problem: Which is bigger, $0.5$ or $0.45$?
steps: Compare from the left. Both have 0 ones.
Tenths - $0.5$ has 5 tenths; $0.45$ has 4 tenths. 5 tenths is more.
We can stop there - the tenths place decides.
Check with hundredths - $0.5 = 0.50$, which is 50 hundredths, against 45 hundredths.
example_harder.answer: $0.5$ is bigger. More digits does not mean bigger.

word.text:
Numbers written with a point and place values for parts are called **decimals** (from Latin *decimus*,
"tenth"). The point is the **decimal point**, and the digits after it are **decimal places**: $3.25$
has two decimal places.

symbols.name: decimal point
symbols.looks_like: A full stop placed between digits, as in 3.25.
symbols.means: Separates the whole-number part (on the left) from the parts of a whole (on the right).
symbols.why: It marks where the ones place is, so every other digit's place is known. In many countries a comma is used instead - 3,25.

formal.statement:
A **decimal** numeral extends base-ten place value to the right of a decimal point: the digits after
the point count tenths, hundredths, thousandths and so on, each place being one tenth of the place to
its left. For example $3.25 = 3 + \tfrac{2}{10} + \tfrac{5}{100}$.

glossary.meaning: Each place is worth ten times the place to its right.
Parts of a whole cut into 10, or into 100, equal pieces.
Ten times smaller than.

notation.read_aloud: three point two five equals three plus two tenths plus five hundredths
notation.english: Three and a quarter - three wholes and twenty-five hundredths.

connections_back.how: Tenths and hundredths are fractions with denominators 10 and 100.
Decimals continue place value to the right.

worked.title: Comparing a third pair
worked.problem: Which is bigger, $0.3$ or $0.25$?
steps: Tenths first - $0.3$ has 3 tenths; $0.25$ has 2 tenths.
3 tenths beats 2 tenths.
worked.answer: $0.3$ is bigger. (As hundredths - 30 against 25.)

experiment.task: Shade the grid to show $0.35$.
experiment.success:
$0.35$ is 3 full rows (3 tenths) and 5 more squares (5 hundredths) - 35 hundredths in all. The digits
after the point tell you exactly what to shade.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking a decimal with more digits is bigger ($0.45 > 0.5$).
mistakes.why: Place value decides - compare tenths first.
mistakes.fix: Line the numbers up at the decimal point and compare from the left. Add zeros if it helps - $0.50$ against $0.45$.

mistakes.mistake: Writing a quarter as $1.4$.
mistakes.why: The decimal point is not a fraction bar.
mistakes.fix: Convert to hundredths first - a quarter is 25 hundredths, $0.25$.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking $0.7$ and $0.70$ are different.
mistakes.why: Adding a zero at the end adds "zero hundredths" - nothing.
mistakes.fix: Trailing zeros after the point do not change the value.

statements.text: The Flemish mathematician Simon Stevin popularised decimal fractions in Europe in his 1585 booklet *De Thiende* ("The Tenth").
Some countries write the decimal point as a comma (3,25) and others as a full stop (3.25).

questions.prompt: Which is bigger, $0.5$ or $0.45$?
questions.explanation: $0.5$ has 5 tenths; $0.45$ has 4 tenths and 5 hundredths. $0.5$ is bigger.

options.diagnosis: Compare tenths first - 5 tenths beats 4 tenths. More digits does not mean bigger.
$0.5 = 0.50$, which is 50 hundredths, not 45.

questions.prompt: True or false: $0.25$ is the same as $\tfrac{1}{4}$.
questions.diagnosis: $0.25$ is 25 hundredths, and 25 of 100 is one quarter.

questions.prompt: Explain what each digit in $4.62$ is worth.
questions.explanation: Ones, then tenths, then hundredths.
rubric: 4 is four ones (wholes).
6 is six tenths.
2 is two hundredths.
questions.model_answer: In $4.62$, the 4 is four wholes, the 6 is six tenths and the 2 is two hundredths - four and sixty-two hundredths.

connections_forward.how: Percentages are hundredths with a different name.
Rounding decimals to estimate.
Endless decimals describe every point on the number line.
Computers store decimals approximately - a source of numerical error.

alternatives.title: A metre stick
alternatives.text:
A metre stick is marked in 100 centimetres. 1 centimetre is $0.01$ metres (one hundredth). 10
centimetres is $0.1$ metres (one tenth). A pencil 15 centimetres long is $0.15$ metres - 1 tenth and 5
hundredths of a metre. Measuring in metres with a centimetre ruler is reading decimals.

alternatives.title: Line them up
alternatives.text:
To compare or read decimals:

1. Write them one above the other with the decimal points lined up.
2. Fill any empty places with 0 so they have the same number of digits after the point.
3. Compare digit by digit from the left, as with whole numbers.

$0.5$ becomes $0.50$; line it up with $0.45$; 5 tenths against 4 tenths - done.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
The dot in a number like 2.5 is like a fence. On the left are whole things - 2 whole apples. On the
right are pieces - 5 tenths of an apple, which is half an apple. So 2.5 is two and a half apples.

l1-divisibility.goal:
We are learning what it means for one number to divide another, the symbol $\mid$, what a remainder is, and
quick tests for divisibility.
l1-divisibility.why:
Divisibility is the central relationship of number theory - primes, greatest common divisors, congruences
and the Riemann Hypothesis all rest on it. The symbol $d \mid n$ appears on almost every page of number
theory research.
l1-divisibility.problem: Can 17 sweets be shared equally among 5 children? If not, how close can we get, and what is left?
l1-divisibility.plain:
We say **5 divides 15** when 15 objects can be shared into **5 equal groups with nothing left over** (3 in
each). Equally, 15 is **divisible by** 5.

Sometimes sharing does not come out exactly. 17 sweets among 5 children: each gets 3 (using 15), and **2
are left over**. The amount left over is the **remainder**. A remainder is always smaller than the number
of groups - if it were not, everyone could have one more.

Divisibility is the same fact as factors and multiples, in different words:

- 5 divides 15 - 5 is a factor of 15 - 15 is a multiple of 5.

**Quick tests** (using the digits):

- **2** divides a number when its last digit is even (0, 2, 4, 6, 8).
- **5** divides it when the last digit is 0 or 5.
- **10** divides it when the last digit is 0.
- **3** divides it when the **sum of its digits** is divisible by 3 - for 123, $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$, so 3 divides
  123.

analogy.title: Dealing cards
analogy.text:
Deal a pack of cards one at a time around a table. If the pack runs out exactly at the last player, the
number of cards was divisible by the number of players. If a few cards are left in your hand that cannot
go all the way round, those are the remainder.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: items dealt one at a time into equal groups, going round and round. When there are not
enough items left to go round once more, the dealing stops. The display shows how many each group got and
how many are left over - the remainder.
visual.prompt: Change the number of items or groups. When is the remainder zero?

example_simple.title: Fifteen among five
example_simple.problem: Does 5 divide 15?
steps: Deal 15 items into 5 groups - each group gets 3.
Nothing is left over.

example_harder.title: Seventeen among five
example_harder.problem: Does 5 divide 17? If not, what is the remainder?
steps: Deal 17 items into 5 groups. After 3 rounds, 15 items are used.
2 items remain - not enough for another round.
The remainder is 2.
example_harder.answer: No - $5 \nmid 17$. The remainder is 2.

word.text:
When one number shares into another exactly, the second is **divisible** by the first, and the first
**divides** the second. What is left when sharing is not exact is the **remainder** (from Latin
*remanere*, "to stay behind").

symbols.name: divides sign
symbols.looks_like: A single short upright line between two numbers, as in $3 \mid 12$.
symbols.means: "Divides" - the left number shares exactly into the right number. A slash through it, $\nmid$, means "does not divide".
symbols.why: Mathematicians needed a compact way to write the most common relationship in number theory.
symbols.read_aloud: "Divides" - $3 \mid 12$ is "three divides twelve". It is NOT a fraction and NOT "three over twelve".

formal.statement:
For integers $d$ and $n$ with $d \neq 0$, we say $d$ **divides** $n$, written $d \mid n$, if $n = d \times k$
for some integer $k$; then $n$ is **divisible** by $d$. For a whole number $n$ and a natural number $d$,
there are unique whole numbers $q$ and $r$ with $n = d \times q + r$ and $0 \le r < d$; the number $r$ is the
**remainder**, and $d \mid n$ exactly when $r = 0$.

glossary.meaning: $d$ is not zero - you cannot share into zero groups.
$n$ items make $d$ groups of $q$, with $r$ left over.
The remainder is at least 0 (the symbol $\le$ means "less than or equal to") and smaller than the number of groups.
There is exactly one such pair $q$ and $r$.

notation.read_aloud: three divides twelve; five does not divide twelve

parts.meaning: Does not divide - the slash means "not".

notation.english: Twelve shares exactly into 3 groups, but not into 5.

notation.read_aloud: seventeen equals five times three plus two

parts.meaning: 5 groups of 3 - the part that shares exactly.

notation.english: Sharing 17 into 5 groups gives 3 each with 2 left over.

connections_back.how: "$d$ divides $n$" is the same as "$d$ is a factor of $n$".
It is also the same as "$n$ is a multiple of $d$".

worked.title: The digit-sum test
worked.problem: Is 123 divisible by 3?
steps: Add the digits - $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$.
6 is divisible by 3.
So by the digit-sum test, 3 divides 123.
Check by sharing - 123 into 3 groups gives 41 each - $123 = 3 \times 41$.
worked.answer: Yes - $3 \mid 123$.

experiment.task: Keep 24 items, and find a number of groups (not 1 and not 24) that shares them with nothing left over.
experiment.success:
Any number of groups that leaves remainder 0 divides 24 - 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12 all work. These are
exactly the factors of 24 (apart from 1 and 24 themselves).

mistakes.mistake: Reading $3 \mid 12$ as the fraction $\tfrac{3}{12}$.
mistakes.why: The upright bar is a statement - "3 divides 12" - not a number.
mistakes.fix: Read it aloud as "divides". $3 \mid 12$ is true; $\tfrac{3}{12}$ is a quarter.

mistakes.mistake: Getting the order wrong - writing $12 \mid 3$ to mean "3 divides 12".
mistakes.why: The divider goes on the left.
mistakes.fix: Say it aloud - "three divides twelve" - and write it in that order.

mistakes.mistake: A remainder bigger than the number of groups.
mistakes.why: If 7 were left from sharing among 5, everyone could have one more.
mistakes.fix: The remainder is always smaller than the number of groups.

statements.text: A number is divisible by 3 exactly when the sum of its digits is divisible by 3. The same is true for 9.
statements.note: This works because 10, 100, 1000, ... each leave remainder 1 on division by 3 and 9. You will prove it with modular arithmetic in Level 10.

statements.text: For any whole number and any number of groups, the quotient and remainder of sharing are unique.
statements.note: This is called the division theorem.

questions.prompt: Which of these numbers are divisible by 5? Choose all that apply.
questions.explanation: A number is divisible by 5 when its last digit is 0 or 5.

options.diagnosis: The last digit is 2, not 0 or 5 - so 5 does not divide 552.
51 ends in 1. (Ending with a 5 at the *start* does not count - only the last digit matters.)

questions.prompt: True or false: $3 \mid 12$ means the fraction three twelfths.
questions.explanation: False. $3 \mid 12$ is the statement "3 divides 12".
questions.diagnosis: The upright bar means "divides". $3 \mid 12$ says 3 divides 12 exactly - a true statement, not a number.

questions.prompt: Explain what $4 \mid 20$ means, and what the remainder is when 22 is shared into 4 groups.
questions.explanation: $4 \mid 20$ because $20 = 4 \times 5$; $22 = 4 \times 5 + 2$, remainder 2.
rubric: $4 \mid 20$ means 20 shares into 4 equal groups with nothing left over (20 = 4 × 5).
22 into 4 groups gives 5 each with 2 left over.
The remainder is 2.
questions.model_answer:
$4 \mid 20$ means "4 divides 20" - 20 can be shared into 4 equal groups of 5 with nothing left over.
Sharing 22 into 4 groups gives 5 each (using 20), so 2 are left over - the remainder is 2.

connections_forward.how: The largest number dividing two numbers.
Remainders as part of division.
Congruences - arithmetic built from divisibility.

alternatives.title: Packing eggs
alternatives.text:
A farmer packs eggs into boxes of 6. With 30 eggs, she fills 5 boxes exactly - 6 divides 30. With 32 eggs,
she fills 5 boxes and has 2 eggs left over - the remainder. She can never have 6 or more left, because
she would simply fill another box.

alternatives.title: Three questions
alternatives.text:
To decide whether $d \mid n$:

1. Share $n$ into $d$ equal groups (deal them out, or skip count by $d$).
2. Look at what is left over.
3. If nothing is left, $d \mid n$. If something is left, $d \nmid n$, and what is left is the remainder.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
You have 10 stickers and 2 friends. Give them out one at a time: one for Sam, one for Lily, one for Sam...
Each friend gets 5 and none are left. So 2 divides 10! With 3 friends, each gets 3 and 1 sticker is left
over - that leftover sticker is called the remainder.

l1-equal-groups.goal:
We are learning to count in equal groups - skip counting by twos, threes and fives - and to see
equal rows as rectangles of objects.
l1-equal-groups.why:
Equal groups are everywhere: pairs of shoes, boxes of eggs, rows of chairs. They are the key to
understanding even and odd numbers, factors, multiples and prime numbers later in this level -
and they are the idea behind multiplication.
l1-equal-groups.problem: If a room has 4 rows of 6 chairs, how can you find the total without counting every chair?
l1-equal-groups.plain:
When things come in **equal groups**, you can count the groups instead of every object.

Four bags with two apples in each? Count in twos: **2, 4, 6, 8**. That is called **skip counting** -
you skip over the numbers in between because each group adds the same amount.

Equal groups can also be laid out in **rows**. Twelve tiles in 3 rows of 4 make a neat rectangle.
Count the rows in fours: 4, 8, 12.

A wonderful fact: turn the rectangle on its side and it becomes 4 rows of 3 - still 12 tiles,
because nothing was added or taken away. So 3 groups of 4 and 4 groups of 3 are the same total.

Mathematicians have a short way to write "3 groups of 4": $3 \times 4$. We will study it properly in
Level 2; for now, read it as "3 groups of 4".

analogy.title: Egg boxes and pairs of socks
analogy.text:
Shops pack eggs in boxes of six so you never have to count eggs one by one: two boxes is twelve
eggs, three boxes is eighteen. Socks come in pairs: five pairs is ten socks. Counting groups
instead of single objects is something you already do without thinking.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: 12 square tiles arranged in equal rows. The control changes how many rows
there are. When the rows come out equal with none left over, the tiles form a perfect
rectangle and the counting-in-groups total is shown beside it.
visual.prompt: Try 2, 3, 4 and 6 rows. Does the total ever change?

example_simple.title: Bags of apples
example_simple.problem: There are 4 bags with 2 apples in each. How many apples are there?
steps: Each bag adds the same amount - 2 apples.
Skip count in twos, once for each bag - 2, 4, 6, 8.

example_harder.title: Turning the rectangle
example_harder.problem: A tray holds biscuits in 3 rows of 5. Your friend turns it to see 5 rows of 3. Who has more biscuits?
steps: Count 3 rows of 5 - 5, 10, 15.
Count 5 rows of 3 - 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.
Turning the tray moved no biscuits, so the totals had to be equal - and they are.
example_harder.answer: Neither - both see 15 biscuits. 3 groups of 5 is the same total as 5 groups of 3.

word.text:
Counting in equal jumps is called **skip counting**. Objects arranged in equal rows and columns
form an **array** (from an old French word meaning "to arrange"). Putting together equal groups is
called **multiplication** - which has its own symbol.

symbols.name: times sign
symbols.looks_like: A small diagonal cross, like the letter x tilted on its side.
symbols.means: "Groups of". $3 \times 4$ means three groups of four (or three rows of four).
symbols.why: Writing "groups of" again and again is slow. The cross was used for multiplication by the English mathematician William Oughtred in 1631.

formal.statement:
An **array** with $r$ rows and $c$ objects in every row contains $r \times c$ objects in total,
found by skip counting by $c$ a total of $r$ times. The total is the same as for an array with
$c$ rows and $r$ objects in every row.

glossary.meaning: Letters standing for "the number of rows" and "the number in each row". Any counting numbers can go here.
Counting c, then c more, then c more again.
r groups of c - the total number of objects.

notation.read_aloud: three times four equals twelve
notation.english: Three groups of four make twelve altogether.

connections_back.how: Bundling in tens was counting in equal groups of ten.
Skip counting makes a pattern - each number is the same amount more than the last.

worked.title: Chairs in a hall
worked.problem: Chairs are set out in 4 rows with 6 chairs in each row. How many chairs are there?
steps: There are 4 equal groups (rows), each of 6.
Skip count by 6, once per row - 6, 12, 18, 24.
worked.answer: 24 chairs. In symbols, $4 \times 6 = 24$.

experiment.task: Arrange the 12 tiles into exactly 4 equal rows.
experiment.success:
4 rows of 3 tiles - $4 \times 3 = 12$. Now turn it sideways in your mind: 3 rows of 4. Same
tiles, same total.

mistakes.mistake: Adding the number of groups to the group size ("3 groups of 4 is 7").
mistakes.why: 3 + 4 counts only one object per group. Each group holds 4 objects.
mistakes.fix: Skip count by the group size, once for each group - 4, 8, 12.

mistakes.mistake: Using groups of different sizes.
mistakes.why: Skip counting only works when every group adds the same amount.
mistakes.fix: Check that every group (row) has the same number before skip counting.

statements.text: An array of 3 rows of 5 has the same number of objects as an array of 5 rows of 3 - and in general, a rows of b equals b rows of a.
statements.note: Turning an array on its side moves no objects. In Level 2 this is called the commutative property of multiplication.

statements.text: The cross $\times$ for multiplication was used by William Oughtred in 1631.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an array?
questions.explanation: An array has equal rows - 3 rows of 5.

options.diagnosis: The rows are not all the same length, so this is not an array.
An array has equal rows and columns - a heap has no rows at all.

questions.prompt: True or false: 3 groups of 5 and 5 groups of 3 make the same total.
questions.explanation: True - both are 15.
questions.diagnosis: Picture 3 rows of 5 and turn it on its side - you get 5 rows of 3 without moving any object.

questions.prompt: There are 5 boxes with 3 pens in each box. How many pens are there?
questions.explanation: Skip count by 3 five times - 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.

common_wrong.diagnosis: 5 + 3 counts the boxes and one box's pens. Each of the 5 boxes holds 3 pens - count 3, 6, 9, 12, 15.

questions.prompt: Explain how to find the number of tiles in 6 rows of 4 without counting every tile, and what $6 \times 4$ means.
questions.explanation: Skip count by the row length once per row; $6 \times 4$ means six groups of four.
rubric: Skip count by 4 (the row length), once for each of the 6 rows.
Gets 24.
$6 \times 4$ means six groups (rows) of four.
questions.model_answer:
Count in fours, once for each row - 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24. So there are 24 tiles. $6 \times 4$
means six groups of four, which is 24.

connections_forward.how: Even numbers are the ones that split into groups of two.
Prime numbers are those that cannot be arranged into a rectangle with more than one row.
The possible numbers of equal rows are called factors.
Multiplication studied fully.

alternatives.title: Clap and count
alternatives.text:
Put your hands out and count in twos while clapping: clap on 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and whisper the
numbers in between (1, 3, 5, 7, 9). Now do it in threes - clap on 3, 6, 9, 12 - whispering the
others. The claps are skip counting: you only "land" on the end of each group.

alternatives.title: Rectangles of dots
alternatives.text:
Draw 3 rows of 4 dots. Now draw a box around each row: three boxes, four dots in each. Count
the dots row by row: 4, 8, 12. Now draw boxes around each column instead: four boxes of three
dots - 3, 6, 9, 12. The same dots, grouped two different ways, give the same total. Equal groups
are just a way of looking at a rectangle.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
You have 3 plates and you put 2 cookies on each plate. How many cookies? Count by twos: 2, 4,
6! Six cookies. Counting by twos (or threes, or fives) is a quick way to count when things come
in groups that are all the same size.

l1-equal-quantities.goal:
We are learning exactly what "equal" means, and the true meaning of the equals sign $=$:
"the two sides are the same amount".
l1-equal-quantities.why:
The equals sign is the most important symbol in mathematics. Every equation - from $2 + 3 = 5$
to the equations of the zeta function - is a claim that two things are equal. Misreading it as
"here comes the answer" is the most common reason algebra later feels confusing.
l1-equal-quantities.problem: What exactly are we claiming when we write $=$, and how can we check that the claim is true?
l1-equal-quantities.plain:
Two quantities are **equal** when they are exactly the same amount. Five apples and five pears are
equal *in number*: they pair off perfectly, with nothing left over.

The **equals sign** $=$ makes a claim: *the thing on the left is the same amount as the thing on
the right*. It works like a **balance scale** - the scale sits level only when both sides hold the
same amount.

This means $=$ is **not** an instruction "work out the answer". These are all true:

- $3 + 2 = 5$
- $5 = 3 + 2$ (the same claim, written the other way round)
- $2 + 3 = 1 + 4$ (neither side is "the answer" - both sides are 5)

And equal things behave sensibly: anything equals itself; if one thing equals a second, the second
equals the first; and if two things both equal a third, they equal each other.

analogy.title: The balance scale
analogy.text:
A balance scale has two pans. Put the same weight on each and the beam sits level; put more on one
side and it tips. The equals sign is a written balance: $2 + 3 = 1 + 4$ says the left pan (2 and 3)
and the right pan (1 and 4) hold exactly the same amount, so the beam is level.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a balance scale with blocks on each pan. The beam tips down toward the
heavier side. When both pans hold the same number of blocks, the beam is level and the statement
underneath shows $=$.
visual.prompt: Add and remove blocks on each side. When is the beam level?

example_simple.title: Five and three-plus-two
example_simple.problem: Is $3 + 2 = 5$ true?
steps: Left side - 3 blocks and 2 more blocks is 5 blocks.
Right side - 5 blocks.
Both sides hold the same amount, so the balance is level.

example_harder.title: No answer on either side
steps: Left side - 2 and 3 more is 5.
Right side - 1 and 4 more is 5.
Both sides are 5, so they are equal - even though neither side is a single "answer".
example_harder.answer: True. The equals sign only claims the two sides are the same amount.

word.text:
Being the same amount is called being **equal**, and the claim that two things are equal is called
an **equality** (or, once letters appear, an **equation**). The two sides are called the
**left-hand side** and **right-hand side**.

symbols.name: equals sign
symbols.looks_like: Two short parallel lines, one above the other.
symbols.means: "Is the same amount as". The left-hand side and the right-hand side are equal.
symbols.why: Robert Recorde invented it in 1557, choosing two parallel lines of the same length because nothing could be more equal.
symbols.read_aloud: "Equals" or "is equal to". $5 = 3 + 2$ is "five equals three plus two".

glossary.meaning: Any numbers at all.
The same amount - collections of each size match one-to-one exactly.
Whenever the first part is true, the second part is also true.

notation.read_aloud: two plus three equals one plus four

parts.meaning: The left-hand side - its amount is 5.
The right-hand side - its amount is also 5.

notation.english: Two and three together is the same amount as one and four together.

connections_back.how: Equal is the case of comparing where nothing is left over.
The equals sign was introduced there; here we look at exactly what it claims.

worked.title: Balance the scale
worked.problem: The left pan has 3 + 5 blocks. How many blocks must go on the right pan to make it level?
steps: The left pan has 3 and 5 more, which is 8 blocks.
For the beam to be level, the right pan needs the same amount.
worked.answer: 8 blocks, so $3 + 5 = 8$.

experiment.task: Change the blocks until the balance is perfectly level.
experiment.success:
The beam is level, so the two sides are equal. Whatever you did - adding to the lighter side or
removing from the heavier - you made the two amounts the same. Algebra will use exactly this idea:
keep the balance level.

mistakes.mistake: Reading "=" as "the answer comes next".
mistakes.why: Then $5 = 3 + 2$ looks wrong and $2 + 3 = 1 + 4$ looks like nonsense - but both are true.
mistakes.fix: Read $=$ as "is the same amount as" every time.

mistakes.mistake: Writing chains like $2 + 3 = 5 + 1 = 6$.
mistakes.why: This claims $2 + 3$ equals $5 + 1$, which is false (5 is not 6).
mistakes.fix: Each $=$ must join two things that really are equal. Write $2 + 3 = 5$ and then $5 + 1 = 6$ separately.

statements.text: For all numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ - $a = a$; if $a = b$ then $b = a$; and if $a = b$ and $b = c$ then $a = c$.
statements.note: These three laws are sometimes taken as the definition of what any "equality" must satisfy.

questions.prompt: True or false: $2 + 3 = 1 + 4$.
questions.explanation: True - both sides are 5.
questions.diagnosis: Work out each side separately - both are 5, so they are equal.

questions.prompt: What number makes this true?  $5 + 2 = \square + 3$
questions.hint: Work out the left side first. Then ask what must be added to 3 to make the same amount.
questions.explanation: The left side is 7. For the right side to be 7, the box must be 4, because $4 + 3 = 7$.

common_wrong.diagnosis: 7 is the value of the left side, but the right side is "something + 3". It must be 7 altogether, so the box is 4.
That adds all the numbers. The two sides must be the same amount - the left is 7, so the box plus 3 must make 7.

questions.prompt: True or false: $9 = 4 + 5$ is wrong, because the answer must come after the equals sign.
questions.explanation: False. $9 = 4 + 5$ is true.
questions.diagnosis: "=" says both sides are the same amount - it does not care which side is a single number.

questions.prompt: A student writes $4 + 4 = 8 + 2 = 10$. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Each $=$ must join equal things. Here $4 + 4$ is 8 but $8 + 2$ is 10, so they are not equal.

options.text: It claims $4 + 4$ equals $8 + 2$, but 8 is not 10.
Nothing is wrong - each step is correct.
options.diagnosis: Every equals sign must join two things that are really equal. $4 + 4$ is 8, but $8 + 2$ is 10.

options.text: You are not allowed to write two equals signs.
options.diagnosis: Several equals signs are allowed, as long as everything joined really is equal, as in $2 + 2 = 4 = 1 + 3$.

questions.prompt: Explain what the equals sign means, and why $6 = 2 + 4$ is a true statement.
questions.explanation: "=" claims both sides are the same amount.
rubric: "=" means the two sides are the same amount (like a level balance).
It does not mean "here comes the answer".
Both sides of $6 = 2 + 4$ are 6.
questions.model_answer:
The equals sign means the left side and the right side are the same amount, like a level
balance. It doesn't mean "the answer comes next". $6 = 2 + 4$ is true because 2 and 4 together
make 6, which is the same as the left side.

connections_forward.how: Equal parts are the basis of fractions.
Reading equalities in more advanced notation.
Equations - equalities with an unknown number - are solved by keeping the balance level.

alternatives.title: A coat-hanger balance
alternatives.text:
Hang two paper cups from the ends of a coat-hanger and hang the hanger from a door handle. Put 5
coins in each cup and the hanger hangs level. Put 2 coins plus 3 coins in one cup, and 1 coin
plus 4 coins in the other: still level. That is $2 + 3 = 1 + 4$. The equals sign is just a way of
writing "the hanger is level".

alternatives.title: Calculator habit versus mathematics
alternatives.text:
On a calculator you press 2, +, 3, = and the answer appears. That makes "=" feel like a button
meaning "show me the answer". But in mathematics, "=" is a *statement*: it claims two things are
the same amount. A calculator could never display $2 + 3 = 1 + 4$, yet it is a perfectly true
mathematical sentence.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
You have 2 red blocks and 3 blue blocks. Your friend has 1 red block and 4 blue blocks. Who has
more? Count: you have 5, your friend has 5. Same! When two things are the same amount, we use the
equals sign: $2 + 3 = 1 + 4$.

l1-even-odd.goal:
We are learning what even and odd numbers are, how to recognise them instantly, and what happens when
they are added together.
l1-even-odd.why:
Even and odd is the simplest way to sort the integers into two families, and it is the setting for many
first proofs. In complexity theory, the "parity" of a list of bits - whether it contains an even or odd
number of 1s - is a famous example in the study of how much computation problems need.
l1-even-odd.problem: Can everyone in a group be paired up with a partner? How can you tell without pairing them all?
l1-even-odd.plain:
A whole number is **even** if that many objects can be split into **pairs** with nothing left over. It is
**odd** if one object is always left without a partner.

- 8 dots make 4 pairs - even.
- 7 dots make 3 pairs with 1 left over - odd.
- **0 is even** - there is nothing left over (and nothing to pair).

**The quick test:** a number is even exactly when its **last digit** is 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. (Why? Every ten
splits into 5 pairs, so only the ones digit can leave something over.)

Along the number line, even and odd numbers **alternate**: 0 even, 1 odd, 2 even, 3 odd, ... This
includes the negatives: $-2$ is even and $-3$ is odd.

**Adding:** even + even is even; odd + odd is even (the two leftover dots pair up with each other!); even
+ odd is odd.

analogy.title: Dancing in pairs
analogy.text:
At a dance where everyone needs a partner, an even number of people can all dance. With an odd number,
one person always waits by the wall. Whether a number is even or odd is just "does everyone get a
partner?"

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: dots arranged in two rows, so that each dot in the top row is paired with the dot
below it. If a dot has no partner, it is highlighted on its own. Change the number of dots and watch
the leftover dot appear and disappear.
visual.prompt: Step from 1 dot up to 10 dots. What pattern do you see?

example_simple.title: Eight
example_simple.problem: Is 8 even or odd?
steps: Make pairs - 2, 4, 6, 8. Four pairs with nothing left over.

example_harder.title: Odd plus odd
example_harder.problem: 7 is odd and 5 is odd. Is 7 + 5 even or odd - and will odd plus odd always behave this way?
steps: 7 dots are 3 pairs and 1 leftover. 5 dots are 2 pairs and 1 leftover.
Put the groups together - 5 pairs, plus the two leftovers.
The two leftovers pair up with each other! So there is nothing left over.
7 + 5 = 12, which is even. The same reasoning works for any two odd numbers, since each has exactly one leftover.
example_harder.answer: Even - and odd plus odd is always even, because the two leftovers always make a pair.

word.text:
Numbers that pair up exactly are **even numbers**; numbers that leave one over are **odd numbers**. Whether
a number is even or odd is called its **parity**.

l1-even-odd.no_symbol_note:
There is no special symbol for "even" or "odd". In Level 4 you will see them written with letters: an even
number as $2k$ and an odd number as $2k + 1$, where $k$ can be any integer.

formal.statement:
An integer $n$ is **even** if $n = 2 \times k$ for some integer $k$, and **odd** if $n = 2 \times k + 1$
for some integer $k$. Every integer is exactly one of the two.

glossary.meaning: A whole number or its negative.
$k$ pairs - two groups of $k$, or $k$ groups of two.
$k$ pairs and one left over.
There is at least one integer $k$ that makes it true.

notation.read_aloud: fourteen equals two times seven
notation.english: Fourteen is even.

notation.read_aloud: fifteen equals two times seven plus one
notation.english: Fifteen is odd.

connections_back.how: Even numbers are exactly the numbers that split into equal groups of two.
Every integer, including negatives and zero, is even or odd.

worked.title: The big number
worked.problem: Is 3,457,286 even or odd?
steps: Pairing three million objects is not practical - use the last-digit test.
The last digit is 6.
worked.answer: Even.

experiment.task: Change the number of dots to an odd number, and notice what happens to the pairs.
experiment.success:
One dot is left without a partner - that is what makes the number odd. Add one more dot and it finds a
partner: the next number is even. Even and odd always alternate.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking 0 is not even.
mistakes.why: 0 objects leave nothing over, and $0 = 2 \times 0$.
mistakes.fix: Zero is even - it sits between the odd numbers $-1$ and 1.

mistakes.mistake: Looking at the first digit instead of the last.
mistakes.why: Only the ones digit can leave something over - every ten splits into pairs.
mistakes.fix: Check the last digit - 34 is even, 43 is odd.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking negative numbers are not even or odd.
mistakes.why: The definitions work for all integers - $-6 = 2 \times (-3)$.
mistakes.fix: Use the same rules - $-6$ is even, $-7$ is odd.

statements.text: The sum of two odd numbers is always even.
statements.note: Each odd number has exactly one leftover, and the two leftovers pair up.

statements.text: The sum of an even number and an odd number is always odd.

questions.prompt: True or false: 0 is an even number.
questions.explanation: True.
questions.diagnosis: Zero objects leave nothing over, and $0 = 2 \times 0$ - so zero is even.

questions.prompt: Without calculating, is 37 + 85 even or odd?
questions.explanation: Odd plus odd is always even (the total is 122).

options.diagnosis: Both numbers are odd. Each has one leftover, and the two leftovers pair up - so the total is even.

questions.prompt: Explain why the sum of two even numbers is always even.
questions.explanation: Pairs joined to pairs are still pairs.
rubric: Each even number can be split into pairs with nothing left over.
Joining two collections of pairs gives only pairs - nothing left over.
So the total is even, whatever the two even numbers are.
questions.model_answer:
An even number of dots splits into pairs with none left over. If you join two such groups, you just get
more pairs - there is still nothing left over. So the total is even, no matter which even numbers you
started with.

connections_forward.how: Classic first proofs are about even and odd numbers.
Even and odd is arithmetic "modulo 2" - remainders on division by 2.
The parity function is a famous example in circuit complexity.

alternatives.title: Socks
alternatives.text:
Grab a handful of socks from a basket and pair them up. If every sock finds a partner, you had an even
number. If one sock is left alone, you had an odd number. You have been testing parity every laundry
day.

alternatives.title: The zebra number line
alternatives.text:
Colour the integers on a number line: even ones dark, odd ones light. You get a perfectly striped
"zebra": dark, light, dark, light - in both directions from zero. Every step of one changes the colour.
That striping is why the last-digit test works and why even and odd alternate forever.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
If you and your friends hold hands in twos and nobody is left out, there's an even number of you. If one
friend has nobody to hold hands with, there's an odd number. That's it!

l1-factors.goal:
We are learning what the factors of a number are - all the numbers of equal rows its objects can be
arranged into - and how to find every factor without missing any.
l1-factors.why:
Factors describe how a number is built. They are needed for simplifying fractions, finding greatest common
divisors, and later for the arithmetic functions that count and add factors - the raw material of Dirichlet
series and the zeta function.
l1-factors.problem: In how many different ways can 12 chairs be set out in equal rows? Which row sizes work?
l1-factors.plain:
A **factor** of a number is a number that **divides it exactly** - that many equal rows can be made with
nothing left over.

For 12 tiles, the rows that work are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12. Those are the **factors of 12**.

Factors come in **pairs**: 2 rows of 6 means 6 rows of 2 also works. So 12's factors pair up:
1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4.

**Finding all factors systematically:** test 1, 2, 3, ... in order. Each time one works, write down it
*and* its partner. Stop when the numbers you are testing meet the partners you have already found.

Every number has at least two factors, 1 and itself. **Prime numbers have exactly two.**

analogy.title: Setting out chairs
analogy.text:
A teacher with 12 chairs can set them out in 1 long row, or 2 rows of 6, or 3 rows of 4, or 4 rows of 3,
or 6 rows of 2, or 12 rows of 1. Each possible number of rows is a factor of 12. A number of rows that
leaves a chair spare - like 5 - is not a factor.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: tiles and a control for the number of rows. Every number of rows that gives a perfect
rectangle is recorded in the list of factors, together with its partner (the number of tiles in each row).
visual.prompt: Try every number of rows from 1 to 12. Which ones go in the list?

example_simple.title: Factors of 6
example_simple.problem: Find all the factors of 6.
steps: 1 works (1 row of 6). Partner 6.
2 works (2 rows of 3). Partner 3.
3 is already a partner, so we have met the partners - stop.

example_harder.title: Factors of 36
example_harder.problem: Find all the factors of 36.
steps: 1 and 36. 2 and 18. 3 and 12. 4 and 9.
5 does not work - 36 shared into 5 equal rows leaves 1 over.
6 works - and its partner is 6 itself (6 rows of 6, a square).
The testing number has met its partner, so stop.
example_harder.answer: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36 - nine factors. Because 6 pairs with itself, 36 has an odd number of factors.

word.text:
A number that divides another exactly is a **factor** of it (from Latin *factor*, "maker" - factors
"make" the number). Another word for factor is **divisor**. Two factors that multiply to the number, like
3 and 4 for 12, are a **factor pair**.

l1-factors.no_symbol_note:
The relationship "is a factor of" has its own symbol, a vertical bar - $3 \mid 12$ - which you will meet in
[[lesson:l1-divisibility|Divisibility]]. Factor pairs are written with the times sign: $12 = 3 \times 4$.

formal.statement:
A natural number $d$ is a **factor** (or **divisor**) of an integer $n$ if $n = d \times k$ for some
integer $k$. Factors come in pairs $d$ and $k$ with $d \times k = n$.

glossary.meaning: The candidate factor - the number of equal rows.
$n$ objects make $d$ rows of $k$.
There is a whole number that makes it work - the row length.

notation.read_aloud: twelve equals one times twelve equals two times six equals three times four
notation.english: Every rectangle 12 tiles can make, written as factor pairs.

connections_back.how: A number has a factor other than 1 and itself exactly when it is composite.
Factors are the numbers of equal groups.

worked.title: Factors of 20
worked.problem: List all the factors of 20.
steps: 1 and 20. 2 and 10.
3 does not work (2 left over).
4 and 5.
The next number to test is 5, which is already a partner - stop.

experiment.task: Find every factor of 24 by testing each number of rows.
experiment.success:
24 has eight factors - 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24 - in four pairs. Notice you only needed to test up to 4;
after that, every factor you found was already a partner.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting 1 and the number itself.
mistakes.why: One long row and rows of one always work.
mistakes.fix: Start every list with 1 and the number.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing factors with multiples.
mistakes.why: Factors go *into* a number (they are at most the number); multiples are what you land on by skip counting (at least the number).
mistakes.fix: Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Multiples of 12 are 12, 24, 36, ...

mistakes.mistake: Stopping too early or too late.
mistakes.why: Without a system it is easy to miss a pair.
mistakes.fix: Test in order and write each factor with its partner; stop when they meet.

statements.text: A natural number has an odd number of factors exactly when it can be arranged as a square array (like 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36).
statements.note: Factors come in pairs, except that a square array pairs its side length with itself.

questions.prompt: True or false: 1 is a factor of every natural number.
questions.explanation: True - every number is 1 row of itself.
questions.diagnosis: Any number of tiles can be laid out as one long row - so 1 always divides it.

questions.prompt: How many factors does the prime number 7 have?
questions.explanation: A prime has exactly two factors - 1 and itself.

common_wrong.diagnosis: Both 1 and 7 itself are factors of 7.

questions.prompt: Describe a method for finding all the factors of a number so that you never miss one.
questions.explanation: Test in order, record pairs, stop when they meet.
rubric: Test each number in order, starting from 1.
When a number works, also record its partner (the number it pairs with).
Stop when the numbers being tested reach the partners already found.
questions.model_answer:
Test 1, 2, 3 and so on in order. Whenever one divides the number exactly, write it down together with
its partner. Stop when the number you are about to test is already in your list as a partner - then
every factor has been found.

connections_forward.how: The opposite view - numbers that a given number goes into.
Factors two numbers share.
Counting and adding factors defines important functions in number theory.

alternatives.title: A rainbow of pairs
alternatives.text:
Write the factors of 36 in a row: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 12, 18, 36. Draw an arc joining 1 to 36, another
joining 2 to 18, then 3 to 12, then 4 to 9. The 6 in the middle has no partner but itself. The arcs make a
rainbow - and the rainbow shows why you can stop searching once you reach the middle.

alternatives.title: Can I share it equally?
alternatives.text:
For each number from 1 to 12, ask: "Can I share 12 sweets equally among this many people, with none
left?" 1 person - yes. 2 - yes (6 each). 3 - yes (4 each). 4 - yes (3 each). 5 - no. 6 - yes. 7, 8, 9, 10,
11 - no. 12 - yes (1 each). The "yes" answers are the factors.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
You have 6 cookies. Can you share them fairly with 2 friends? Yes, 3 each! With 3 friends? Yes, 2 each!
With 4 friends? No - 2 would be left over. The numbers of friends that work - 1, 2, 3 and 6 - are called
the factors of 6.

l1-fractions.goal:
We are learning what a fraction is - a number describing some equal parts of a whole - and where
fractions live on the number line.
l1-fractions.why:
Many quantities fall between whole numbers: half a cake, three quarters of an hour, a rope 2½ metres
long. Fractions fill the gaps between the integers. Infinite sums of fractions, like
$1 + \tfrac{1}{2} + \tfrac{1}{3} + \cdots$, eventually lead to the Riemann zeta function itself.
l1-fractions.problem: When a pizza is shared and you get some of the slices, what number describes how much you got?
l1-fractions.plain:
Cut a whole into **equal parts**. A **fraction** says how many of those parts you have.

If a pizza is cut into **8 equal slices** and you take **3**, you have **three-eighths** of the pizza,
written $\tfrac{3}{8}$.

- The **bottom** number says how many equal parts make the whole (8).
- The **top** number says how many of those parts you have (3).

The parts **must be equal**. If one slice is huge and another tiny, "one slice" is not a fair eighth.

Fractions are numbers, so they have places on the number line - **between** the integers. $\tfrac{1}{2}$
sits halfway from 0 to 1. Fractions can also be bigger than one: $\tfrac{5}{4}$ is five quarters - one
whole pizza and one more quarter.

And every integer is a fraction too: $3 = \tfrac{3}{1}$ (three wholes, each "cut" into 1 part).

analogy.title: Sharing a pizza
analogy.text:
A pizza cut into 8 equal slices: each slice is one-eighth. Take 3 slices and you have three-eighths.
Your friend takes 5 slices - five-eighths. Together you took $\tfrac{8}{8}$, the whole pizza. The
"eighths" tell you the slice size; the 3 and the 5 count slices.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a circle (a pizza) cut into equal slices, with some slices shaded. The bottom
control sets how many equal slices the whole pizza is cut into; the top control sets how many are
shaded. The fraction shown is "shaded slices over total slices".
visual.prompt: Cut the pizza into different numbers of slices and shade some. When does the shaded part look like exactly half?

example_simple.title: A quarter of a pizza
example_simple.problem: A pizza is cut into 4 equal slices and you eat 1. What fraction did you eat?
steps: The whole is cut into 4 equal parts - the bottom number is 4.
You ate 1 of them - the top number is 1.

example_harder.title: Fractions on the number line
example_harder.problem: Where is $\tfrac{3}{4}$ on the number line?
steps: Look at the stretch from 0 to 1 - one whole.
Cut it into 4 equal parts, making marks at a quarter, a half and three quarters.
Count 3 parts from 0.
example_harder.answer: $\tfrac{3}{4}$ is three quarters of the way from 0 to 1 - more than a half, less than 1.

word.text:
Numbers like these are **fractions**, from Latin *fractio*, "breaking". Mathematicians call every
number that can be written as one integer over another a **rational number** - from "ratio" - and the
set of them is written $\mathbb{Q}$ (for *quotient*, a word for the result of dividing).

symbols.name: fraction bar
symbols.looks_like: One number written above a horizontal line, and another number below it. Sometimes typed with a slash - 3/8.
symbols.means: The whole is cut into $b$ equal parts, and we take $a$ of them.
symbols.why: Writing one number over the other shows clearly that the bottom number shares the whole and the top number counts parts. The horizontal bar was used by Arab mathematicians and popularised in Europe by Fibonacci.
symbols.read_aloud: "Three eighths" or "three over eight" for $\tfrac{3}{8}$; "one half", "one third", "one quarter" for the commonest ones.

symbols.name: blackboard-bold Q
symbols.looks_like: A capital Q with a doubled stroke.
symbols.means: The set of all rational numbers - all fractions of integers.
symbols.why: Q for "quotient".

formal.statement:
A **fraction** is a number written $\tfrac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers and $b \neq 0$.
It represents $a$ parts when one whole is divided into $b$ equal parts. The set of all such numbers
is the set of **rational numbers**, $\mathbb{Q}$. Every integer $n$ is rational, since $n = \tfrac{n}{1}$.

glossary.meaning: Any integers - the top and bottom numbers.
"$b$ is not equal to zero". The slash through the equals sign means "not". A whole cannot be cut into zero parts.
Parts that are all exactly the same size.
Any integer $n$ is $n$ wholes, each counted as one part out of one.

notation.read_aloud: three eighths

parts.meaning: How many parts we have - the numerator (next lesson).
How many equal parts make one whole - the denominator.

notation.english: Three of the eight equal parts of a whole.

connections_back.how: Fractions depend on parts being exactly equal.
Fractions are points between the integers on the number line.
When a unit does not fit an exact number of times, fractions measure the leftover.

worked.title: A chocolate bar
worked.problem: A chocolate bar has 12 equal pieces. You eat 5. What fraction of the bar did you eat, and what fraction is left?
steps: The whole bar is 12 equal pieces - the bottom number is 12.
You ate 5 - so you ate $\tfrac{5}{12}$.
7 pieces are left - $\tfrac{7}{12}$ of the bar remains.
Check - 5 twelfths and 7 twelfths make 12 twelfths, the whole bar.
worked.answer: You ate $\tfrac{5}{12}$; $\tfrac{7}{12}$ is left.

experiment.task: Make exactly three quarters of a pizza.
experiment.success:
Three quarters - and if you used 8 slices with 6 shaded, or 12 with 9, that is three quarters too.
Different-looking fractions can be the same amount; the next lesson explains why.

mistakes.mistake: Ignoring whether the parts are equal.
mistakes.why: A fraction only makes sense if every part is the same size.
mistakes.fix: Check the parts are equal before naming the fraction.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking $\tfrac{1}{8}$ is bigger than $\tfrac{1}{4}$ because 8 is bigger than 4.
mistakes.why: Cutting into more parts makes each part *smaller*.
mistakes.fix: Picture the pizzas - one slice of 8 is thinner than one slice of 4.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking whole numbers are not fractions.
mistakes.why: $3 = \tfrac{3}{1}$ - every integer can be written as a fraction.
mistakes.fix: Remember the families are nested - integers sit inside the rational numbers.

statements.text: The Rhind Mathematical Papyrus, written in Egypt around 1550 BCE, contains tables and problems using fractions.
Between any two different fractions there is another fraction.
statements.note: For example, halfway between them. So the fractions, unlike the integers, have no "next" fraction.

questions.prompt: A cake is cut into 4 pieces of very different sizes. Is one piece "one quarter" of the cake?
questions.explanation: Fractions are about equal parts. Unequal pieces are not quarters.

options.text: Not necessarily - quarters must be equal parts.
Yes - there are 4 pieces, so each is a quarter.
options.diagnosis: A fraction counts equal parts. Unequal pieces are not quarters.

questions.prompt: True or false: the integer 3 can be written as the fraction $\tfrac{3}{1}$.
questions.explanation: True - every integer is a rational number.
questions.diagnosis: Three wholes, each counted as one part out of one, is $\tfrac{3}{1}$.

questions.prompt: Explain what $\tfrac{2}{5}$ means, using a picture or example in words.
questions.explanation: The bottom number counts equal parts in the whole; the top counts parts taken.
rubric: The whole is divided into 5 equal parts.
We take (shade) 2 of those parts.
Gives a concrete example such as a bar or pizza.
questions.model_answer: $\tfrac{2}{5}$ means a whole cut into 5 equal parts with 2 of them taken - like a chocolate bar of 5 equal pieces where you eat 2.

connections_forward.how: The names and roles of the top and bottom numbers.
Another way to write fractions, using place value.
Adding and multiplying fractions.
Adding infinitely many fractions - the road to the zeta function.

alternatives.title: Fold a sheet of paper
alternatives.text:
Fold a sheet of paper in half and open it - two equal parts. Colour one: you have coloured
$\tfrac{1}{2}$. Fold another sheet in half and then in half again - four equal parts. Colour three:
$\tfrac{3}{4}$. Folding guarantees the parts are equal, which is exactly what a fraction requires.

alternatives.title: On the ruler
alternatives.text:
Look at a ruler between 0 and 1 centimetre. There are small marks dividing it into 10 equal parts
(millimetres). The 3rd mark is $\tfrac{3}{10}$ of a centimetre. Fractions are simply the points
between the whole-number marks - the number line was full of them all along.

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
You and three friends share a pizza. Cut it into 4 equal slices - one for each of you. Each slice is
one quarter, $\tfrac{1}{4}$. If you sneak one more slice, you've had two quarters - $\tfrac{2}{4}$,
which is half the pizza!

l1-greatest-common-divisor.goal:
We are learning what the greatest common divisor of two numbers is, how to find it by listing factors,
and what it is useful for.
l1-greatest-common-divisor.why:
The greatest common divisor (GCD) simplifies fractions and solves sharing problems. It also has one of the
oldest algorithms in mathematics - Euclid's algorithm, more than 2,000 years old - which is a classic first
example in the study of how fast algorithms run.
l1-greatest-common-divisor.problem:
You have 12 red beads and 18 blue beads and want to make identical bags using every bead. What is the
largest number of identical bags you can make?
l1-greatest-common-divisor.plain:
A **common divisor** (or common factor) of two numbers is a number that divides **both** of them.

- Factors of 12 - 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
- Factors of 18 - 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18.
- Common factors - **1, 2, 3, 6**.

The **greatest** of the common divisors is the **greatest common divisor**: for 12 and 18 it is **6**.

For the beads: each bag must get the same number of red beads, so the number of bags must divide 12; and
likewise it must divide 18. The largest possible number of bags is the GCD - 6 bags, each with 2 red and
3 blue beads.

When the GCD of two numbers is 1, they share no factor except 1, and are called **coprime** - for example
8 and 15.

The GCD also **simplifies fractions**: divide the top and bottom of $\tfrac{12}{18}$ by 6 to get
$\tfrac{2}{3}$, the simplest form.

analogy.title: Party bags
analogy.text:
Making identical party bags from 24 sweets and 36 stickers, with nothing left over: the number of bags has
to share both piles exactly. The biggest number of bags that works is the greatest common divisor of 24
and 36 - which is 12 (2 sweets and 3 stickers in each).

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: two overlapping circles. The left holds the factors of the first number, the right
the factors of the second. Factors of both sit in the overlap. The largest number in the overlap is the
greatest common divisor.
visual.prompt: Change the numbers. Can you find two numbers whose overlap contains only 1?

example_simple.title: Eight and twelve
example_simple.problem: Find $\gcd(8, 12)$.
steps: Factors of 8 - 1, 2, 4, 8.
Common factors - 1, 2, 4.
The greatest is 4.

example_harder.title: Simplifying a fraction
example_harder.problem: Write $\tfrac{12}{18}$ in its simplest form.
steps: Find the greatest number dividing both 12 and 18 - $\gcd(12, 18) = 6$.
Divide top and bottom by 6 - think of grouping every 6 small parts into one bigger part.
12 becomes 2 and 18 becomes 3.
example_harder.answer: $\tfrac{12}{18} = \tfrac{2}{3}$, and it cannot be simplified further because $\gcd(2, 3) = 1$.

word.text:
This number is the **greatest common divisor**, often shortened to **GCD**. Some countries call it the
**highest common factor** (HCF) or **greatest common factor** - all the same idea.

symbols.name: GCD notation
symbols.looks_like: The letters gcd followed by two numbers in round brackets, separated by a comma.
symbols.means: The greatest common divisor of the two numbers in the brackets.
symbols.why: A short name for a long phrase. The brackets hold the inputs - the two numbers whose GCD we want.
symbols.read_aloud: "The GCD of $a$ and $b$" - $\gcd(12, 18)$ is "the GCD of twelve and eighteen".

formal.statement:
For integers $a$ and $b$, not both zero, the **greatest common divisor** $\gcd(a, b)$ is the largest natural
number $d$ such that $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$. If $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, then $a$ and $b$ are **coprime**.

glossary.meaning: Every number divides 0, so the GCD of 0 and 0 would not exist.
$d$ divides $a$ exactly.
The biggest of all the common divisors.
Sharing no factor bigger than 1.

notation.read_aloud: the GCD of twelve and eighteen equals six

parts.meaning: The two numbers we are comparing.

notation.english: Six is the biggest number that divides both twelve and eighteen exactly.

connections_back.how: A common divisor divides both numbers.
We find the GCD by comparing lists of factors.

worked.title: Beads in bags
worked.problem: You have 24 red beads and 36 blue beads. What is the largest number of identical bags you can make using all the beads, and what goes in each bag?
steps: The number of bags must divide 24 and must divide 36.
Common factors - 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The greatest is 12.
Sharing 24 red beads into 12 bags gives 2 per bag, and sharing 36 blue beads into 12 bags gives 3 per bag.
worked.answer: 12 bags, each with 2 red and 3 blue beads.

experiment.task: Find the greatest common divisor of 16 and 24 by tapping the largest number in the overlap.
experiment.success:
$\gcd(16, 24) = 8$. Notice that every common factor - 1, 2, 4, 8 - is itself a factor of 8. That is no
accident: every common divisor divides the GCD, a fact you will prove in Level 10.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing a common factor that is not the greatest.
mistakes.why: 2 divides both 12 and 18, but 6 is bigger and also divides both.
mistakes.fix: List *all* the common factors and take the largest.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing the GCD with the least common multiple.
mistakes.why: The GCD goes *into* both numbers (so it is at most the smaller one); a common multiple is something both go into.
mistakes.fix: GCD - smaller than or equal to both numbers. LCM - bigger than or equal to both.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking the GCD must be prime.
mistakes.why: $\gcd(12, 18) = 6$, which is composite.
mistakes.fix: The GCD is simply the greatest common factor, prime or not.

statements.text: Euclid's *Elements* (around 300 BCE) describes a method for finding the greatest common divisor that is still used today - one of the oldest algorithms in existence.
Every common divisor of two numbers divides their greatest common divisor.

questions.prompt: True or false: $\gcd(7, 10) = 1$.
questions.explanation: True - 7 and 10 are coprime.
questions.diagnosis: The factors of 7 are 1 and 7; the factors of 10 are 1, 2, 5 and 10. Only 1 is shared.

questions.prompt: What is $\tfrac{12}{18}$ in its simplest form?
questions.explanation: Dividing top and bottom by $\gcd(12, 18) = 6$ gives $\tfrac{2}{3}$.

options.diagnosis: This is equivalent, but 6 and 9 still share the factor 3. Divide by the GCD, 6, to go straight to the simplest form.
This is equivalent, but 4 and 6 still share the factor 2.

questions.prompt: Explain how to find $\gcd(20, 30)$ and what the answer means.
rubric: List the factors of each number and find the common ones (1, 2, 5, 10).
The greatest common one is 10.
It is the largest number that divides both 20 and 30 exactly.
questions.model_answer:
Factors of 20 are 1, 2, 4, 5, 10, 20; factors of 30 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. The common ones are
1, 2, 5 and 10, so the GCD is 10 - the largest number that divides both 20 and 30 exactly.

connections_forward.how: The partner idea - the smallest common multiple.
Simplifying fractions uses the GCD.
A much faster way to find GCDs - one of the first algorithms ever studied.

alternatives.title: Tiling a rectangle with squares
alternatives.text:
Draw a rectangle 12 squares long and 18 squares wide on squared paper. What is the biggest square tile
that covers it exactly, with no cutting? A 6-by-6 tile fits - 2 tiles along one side and 3 along the
other. A 7-by-7 tile does not fit. The side of the biggest square tile is the GCD of the two side lengths.

alternatives.title: Count down
alternatives.text:
For $\gcd(12, 18)$, ask of each number from 12 downward: "does it divide both?" 12 - divides 12, not 18.
11, 10, 9, 8, 7 - no. 6 - divides 12 (twice) and 18 (three times). Stop! The first "yes" when counting down
is the greatest common divisor. (Counting down from the smaller number guarantees the first success is
the greatest.)

alternatives.title: Like you're five
alternatives.text:
You have 4 apples and 6 bananas, and you want to make fruit bowls that are exactly the same, using all the
fruit. You can make 2 bowls - each with 2 apples and 3 bananas! You can't make 3 identical bowls, or 4. The
biggest number of bowls that works, 2, is called the greatest common divisor.

l1-integers.goal:
We are learning about the integers - all the whole numbers together with their negatives - and the
symbol $\mathbb{Z}$.
l1-integers.why:
The integers are the numbers of number theory. Primes, divisibility and congruences are all about
integers, and research papers say "let $n \in \mathbb{Z}$" constantly. The integers are also the first
number system where every number has both a next number and a previous one.
l1-integers.problem: How do we name the collection of all the evenly spaced points on the number line - in both directions?
l1-integers.plain:
Take the whole numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, ... and add their negatives $-1, -2, -3, \ldots$ The result is the
**integers**:

$$\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$

On the number line, the integers are the **evenly spaced tick marks in both directions**, with nothing
in between. Numbers with parts, like $2.5$ or $-\tfrac{1}{2}$, are not integers - they sit between the
marks.

Every integer has a **next** integer (one more) and a **previous** integer (one less). Unlike the
natural numbers, the integers have no first member: they go on forever in both directions.

The set of integers is written $\mathbb{Z}$.

analogy.title: Floors of a tall building with basements
analogy.text:
A building with many basement levels has floors ..., $-3$, $-2$, $-1$, 0 (ground), 1, 2, 3, ... There
are no half-floors. The lift can always go one floor up or one floor down. The integers are that
building, imagined with no top floor and no bottom floor.

visual.caption:
What you are seeing: a number line from $-8$ to 8 with every integer marked by a highlighted dot. The
movable point can also stop halfway between integers. When it sits on a highlighted dot, its value is
an integer; between dots, it is not.
visual.prompt: Move the point onto integers and between them. Which positions are integers?

example_simple.title: Listing integers
example_simple.problem: List the integers from $-3$ to 3.
steps: Start at $-3$ and step right one at a time.

example_harder.title: How many from minus five to five?
example_harder.problem: How many integers are there from $-5$ to 5, including both ends?
steps: Negative ones - $-5, -4, -3, -2, -1$ - five integers.
Zero - one integer.
Positive ones - $1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ - five integers.
Total - 5, then 1 more, then 5 more.
example_harder.answer: 11 integers. (Forgetting zero gives 10 - a very common slip.)

word.text:
These numbers are the **integers**, from Latin *integer*, meaning "whole" or "untouched". The symbol
$\mathbb{Z}$ comes from the German word *Zahlen*, meaning "numbers".

symbols.name: blackboard-bold Z
symbols.looks_like: A capital Z with its diagonal stroke doubled.
symbols.means: The set of all integers.
symbols.why: Z for the German *Zahlen*, "numbers". German mathematicians were very influential when the notation settled.

formal.statement:
The **integers** form the set $\mathbb{Z} = \{\ldots, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$, consisting of
the whole numbers together with their negatives.

glossary.meaning: The set containing every integer - the dots on both sides mean the list continues forever in both directions.
The opposites $-1, -2, -3, \ldots$
